# 1. Introduction

## 1.1. Background

Forest landscapes are dynamic systems whose ecological functioning depends not only on the total amount of forest habitat, but also on its spatial configuration. A landscape may retain a relatively large forest area while becoming increasingly divided into smaller and more isolated patches. Conversely, forest expansion may progressively reconnect previously separated patches and increase landscape connectivity. Consequently, changes in forest cover and changes in forest fragmentation need to be considered jointly when assessing long-term landscape dynamics.

Across Europe, forest landscapes have followed contrasting trajectories during the last decades. Some regions have experienced forest expansion following agricultural abandonment, rural depopulation and natural vegetation succession, whereas others have been strongly affected by timber harvesting, forest management and repeated disturbance. These contrasted processes provide an opportunity to investigate whether different land-use trajectories can be detected through reproducible landscape metrics.

This project investigates changes in forest habitat amount and spatial configuration between 1990 and 2018 using CORINE Land Cover (CLC) data. Particular attention is given to two contrasting European regions: Spain and the Baltic States — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

## 1.2. Contrasting forest trajectories in Europe

### 1.2.1. Forest expansion and forest transition in Spain

Spain represents a particularly relevant case of long-term forest transition. Following centuries of forest exploitation and land conversion, the twentieth century was characterized by extensive afforestation and reforestation programmes. More than five million hectares were reforested through large-scale public policies between the late nineteenth and early twenty-first centuries, substantially contributing to the expansion of forested land in Spain (Vadell, de-Miguel, and Pemán 2016).

More recent forest expansion, however, cannot be explained by plantations alone. Agricultural abandonment and rural depopulation have allowed spontaneous ecological succession on former cropland and pastures. In Catalonia, the long-term reconstruction of land use between 1868 and 2005 revealed a transition from previous deforestation towards forest expansion, particularly after the 1950s, as forests progressively colonized abandoned agricultural and grazing land (Cervera et al. 2019).

A similar process has been documented at a larger regional scale in Central-North Spain. Velázquez et al. (2022) investigated approximately 9.4 million hectares and identified 145,193 ha of former agricultural land that had naturally regenerated into forests or woodlands. Their study relates this process to rural–urban migration and the abandonment of marginal agricultural land, followed by progressive revegetation from shrubland towards woodland and forest.

Spontaneous forest expansion is therefore now an important land-use process in Mediterranean landscapes. It may have substantial consequences for landscape structure because the colonization of abandoned land can enlarge existing forest patches or connect previously isolated patches, potentially producing processes of forest coalescence (Varela et al. 2020).

For this project, Spain consequently represents a landscape trajectory in which forest expansion and progressive reconnection of forest patches may be expected in at least some regions, although this pattern is not assumed to occur uniformly across the country.

### 1.2.2. Forest disturbance and harvesting in the Baltic States

The Baltic States represent a contrasting forest context. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania contain extensive forest resources, but their forest landscapes have also been strongly influenced by timber harvesting and major socioeconomic transformations since the end of the Soviet period.

Using the full Landsat archive, Potapov et al. (2015) reconstructed forest-cover dynamics across Eastern Europe between 1985 and 2012. Their results highlighted the Baltic region as one of the areas characterized by particularly intensive forest disturbance and harvesting during the post-Soviet period. The study is especially relevant to the present analysis because its observation period closely overlaps the 1990–2018 CORINE time series examined here.

More recent research also points to an intensification of harvesting in parts of Europe. Ceccherini et al. (2020) detected a marked increase in harvested forest area after 2015 and identified northern and Baltic European countries among the areas contributing substantially to this pattern. The authors associated these changes with increasing demand for wood and wood-based products, although interpretation of satellite-derived forest losses remains sensitive to harvesting cycles and subsequent regrowth.

The forestry sector also has considerable economic importance in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Wood pellets are exported from the Baltic region, and the use of woody biomass as renewable energy has contributed to debates concerning the intensity and sustainability of forest exploitation (Kirchner 2022). This relationship should nevertheless not be interpreted as a simple causal chain from pellet production to permanent deforestation, since harvested stands may subsequently regenerate and forest products supply several markets besides bioenergy.

Importantly, the Baltic trajectory is not simply one of continuous forest loss. Long-term research along the Latvian–Russian border shows that forest expansion on abandoned agricultural land can occur simultaneously with intensive forest harvesting. Rendenieks et al. (2020), using historical Corona imagery and Landsat data, documented major changes in forest cover between the late 1960s and 2015 and demonstrated the importance of both agricultural abandonment and changing forest-management regimes.

The Baltic States should therefore be interpreted as landscapes characterized by a combination of forest harvesting, disturbance, regrowth and post-agricultural forest expansion, rather than simply as examples of permanent deforestation.

## 1.3. Scientific rationale

The comparison between Spain and the Baltic States is therefore not intended to oppose a region of “reforestation” to a region of “deforestation”. Instead, the two study areas represent contrasting trajectories of forest landscape transformation.

In parts of Spain, agricultural abandonment and long-term forest transition may favour the expansion and coalescence of forest patches. In the Baltic States, intensive timber harvesting may produce stronger patch turnover and temporary fragmentation, while forest regeneration and agricultural abandonment may simultaneously create new forest cover.

This distinction is particularly important when using CORINE Land Cover. A forest patch that disappears from one CLC observation does not necessarily represent permanent deforestation. For example, an area classified as broad-leaved, coniferous or mixed forest may temporarily become transitional woodland-shrub (CLC class 324) following harvesting or disturbance and later return to a forest class. The analysis therefore focuses on forest habitat amount and fragmentation dynamics, rather than interpreting every forest-class loss as permanent deforestation.

## 1.4. Research question

**How did forest habitat amount and spatial fragmentation evolve between 1990 and 2018 in selected landscapes of Spain and the Baltic States, and do these two regions display contrasting trajectories of forest landscape change?**

## 1.5. Hypotheses

Based on the scientific literature, two broad hypotheses are investigated. These hypotheses describe expected tendencies rather than predefined outcomes.

### 1.5.1 H1 — Forest expansion and coalescence in Spain

In Spanish landscapes affected by agricultural abandonment and natural forest succession, forest habitat amount is expected to increase over time.

If newly forested areas expand around or between existing patches, this process may also reduce fragmentation. The expected landscape-metric response is therefore:

-   **PLAND** may increase, indicating a larger proportion of forest habitat;
-   **LPI** may increase as large forest patches expand or merge;
-   **NP** or **PD** may decrease if formerly isolated patches become connected;
-   **ED** may eventually decrease where patch coalescence reduces the relative amount of forest edge;
-   structural connectivity metrics such as **CONNECT** or **COHESION** may increase.

These changes are not expected to occur systematically in every sampled landscape because fire, urbanization, forestry and local land-use histories can generate different trajectories.

### 1.5.2. H2 — Stronger forest disturbance and patch turnover in the Baltic States

Baltic forest landscapes are expected to show a stronger spatial signature of forest harvesting and disturbance.

Where harvesting temporarily removes or subdivides existing forest stands, the expected response may include:

-   locally stable or decreasing **PLAND**;
-   decreasing **LPI** if large continuous forest patches are subdivided;
-   increasing **NP** or **PD**;
-   increasing **ED** due to the creation of new forest–matrix boundaries;
-   decreasing connectivity.

However, forest regeneration and the colonization of abandoned agricultural land may partly or completely counteract these effects. The Baltic trajectory may therefore be characterized more accurately by high forest-cover turnover and heterogeneous local trajectories than by a uniform decline in forest area.

## 1.6. Objectives

The project has five main objectives:

1.  **Develop a reproducible geoprocessing workflow** capable of automatically retrieving, processing and analysing CORINE Land Cover data for different European regions and years.

2.  **Describe broad European land-cover change** between 1990 and 2018 using interactive CORINE Land Cover maps at Levels 1 and 3.

3.  **Compare forest landscape dynamics in two contrasting European study regions**, Spain and the Baltic States, selected on the basis of documented differences in land-use and forest-management trajectories.

4.  **Quantify temporal changes in forest habitat amount and spatial configuration** within standardized landscape units using complementary landscape metrics such as PLAND, patch density, edge density, largest patch index and connectivity or cohesion.

5.  **Assess whether the observed trajectories are consistent with expectations from the scientific literature**, while explicitly considering uncertainty related to spatial resolution, CORINE classification, temporal sampling and the choice of analytical scale.

## 1.7. General workflow

The analysis follows a reproducible sequence:

**CORINE data acquisition → European land-cover exploration → selection of contrasting study regions → forest habitat reclassification → construction of standardized landscape units → reproducible landscape sampling → landscape-metric calculation → temporal analysis → comparison of regional trajectories.**

All major analytical settings, including years, study regions, forest classes and landscape-unit size, are defined as parameters at the beginning of this Quarto document. This allows the workflow to be adapted to another European region without rewriting the main analysis.

# 1.8. Project initialization

This section initializes the computational environment and prepares the reproducible project structure used throughout the analysis.

The objective is to ensure that the complete workflow can be reproduced after cloning the GitHub repository on another computer. No computer-specific working directory is used: all paths are constructed relative to the project root.

## 1.9. Packages and project parameters

The workflow combines reproducible project management, raster and vector geoprocessing, landscape ecology, interactive visualization, access to the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service API and version-control diagnostics.

The main spatial packages are `sf` for vector data, `terra` for raster processing and `landscapemetrics` for landscape metrics. `giscoR` provides European administrative boundaries, while `here` and `fs` are used to construct portable file paths and manage the project directory structure.

Missing packages are automatically installed and loaded with `pacman::p_load()`.

```{r}
#| label: shiny-shared-setup
#| context: setup
#| include: false
#| cache: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({

  library(leaflet)
  library(terra)
})
```

paths <- list(

    "data_input",
    "corine"
  ),

# ============================================================
# 3. PARAMETERS FROM YAML
# ============================================================

study_areas <- as.character(
  unlist(params$study_areas)
)

spain_countries <- as.character(
  unlist(countries$Spain)
)

baltic_countries <- as.character(
  unlist(countries$Baltic_States)
)

all_countries <- c(
  spain_countries,
  baltic_countries
)

  unlist(params$years)
)

grid_km <- as.numeric(
  params$grid_km
)

  params$habitat_focus
)
