```{r}
  unlist(params$forest_classes)
)

# ============================================================
# 4. COUNTRY-CODE CORRESPONDENCE
# ============================================================

# ISO3 codes are used for the analytical definition of the
# study areas, whereas the CLMS downloads stored locally use
# two-letter country codes.
#
# The Baltic States are treated as ONE study area composed of
# Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

country_lookup <- tibble::tribble(

  ~iso3, ~clms_code, ~study_area,

  "ESP", "ES", "Spain",
  "EST", "EE", "Baltic States",
  "LVA", "LV", "Baltic States",
  "LTU", "LT", "Baltic States"
)

# ============================================================
# 5. GENERIC CORINE RASTER LOADER
# ============================================================
load_clc <- function(
  country_code,
  year
) {

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Locate country/year folder
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  year_folder <- fs::path(
    paths$corine,
    country_code,
    as.character(year)
  )


  if (!fs::dir_exists(year_folder)) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "CORINE directory not found for ",
        country_code,
        " / ",
        year,
        ":\n",
        year_folder
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Search recursively for extracted GeoTIFF
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  tif_files <- fs::dir_ls(
    year_folder,
    regexp = "\\.(tif|tiff)$",
    recurse = TRUE,
    type = "file",
    fail = FALSE
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Validate result
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  if (length(tif_files) == 0) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "No CORINE GeoTIFF found for ",
        country_code,
        " / ",
        year,
        "."
      )
    )
  }


  if (length(tif_files) > 1) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "More than one CORINE GeoTIFF was found for ",
        country_code,
        " / ",
        year,
        ". The dataset structure should be checked."
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Load raster
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  terra::rast(
    tif_files[[1]]
  )
}

# ============================================================
# 6. ANALYTICAL CONFIGURATION SUMMARY
# ============================================================

analysis_parameters <- tibble::tibble(

  parameter = c(
    "Study areas",
    "Spain country code",
    "Baltic country codes",
    "Years",
    "Landscape-unit size",
    "Habitat focus",
    "CORINE forest classes"
  ),

  value = c(
    paste(study_areas, collapse = " vs. "),
    paste(spain_countries, collapse = ", "),
    paste(baltic_countries, collapse = ", "),
    paste(years, collapse = ", "),
    paste0(grid_km, " × ", grid_km, " km"),
    habitat_focus,
    paste(forest_classes, collapse = ", ")
  )
)

analysis_parameters
```

# 2. Reproducible project structure

## 2.1. Project directory organization

A standardized directory structure is created at the beginning of the workflow to separate input data, generated outputs and temporary computational files. This organization improves reproducibility by ensuring that all subsequent operations refer to predefined relative paths rather than to directories manually created on a specific computer.

Three main components are distinguished:

-   `data_input/` contains the source spatial datasets required by the analysis, including CORINE Land Cover data and administrative boundaries;
-   `data_output/` contains products generated by the workflow, such as figures, maps and statistical tables;
-   `cache/` stores temporary computational files that can be recreated and therefore do not need to be versioned.

Because Git does not track empty directories, a `.gitkeep` placeholder is automatically created in directories that need to remain part of the repository structure. The `cache/` directory is excluded from this mechanism because it contains only temporary files.



The diagnostic table verifies that each required directory has been successfully created. The `git_placeholder` column additionally indicates whether a `.gitkeep` file is present. A missing placeholder for `cache/` is expected because this directory contains temporary computational files and is deliberately excluded from version control.

## 2.2. Expected project structure

After initialization, the project follows the directory organization shown below:

``` text
habitat-fragmentation-europe/
│
├── Workflow.qmd
├── .gitignore
│
├── data_input/
│   ├── .gitkeep
│   │
│   ├── corine/
│   │   └── .gitkeep
│   │
│   └── boundaries/
│       └── .gitkeep
│
├── data_output/
│   ├── .gitkeep
│   │
│   ├── figures/
│   │   └── .gitkeep
│   │
│   ├── maps/
│   │   └── .gitkeep
│   │
│   └── tables/
│       └── .gitkeep
│
└── cache/
```

This separation between inputs and outputs is maintained throughout the workflow. Raw CORINE datasets downloaded later from the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service are stored under `data_input/corine/`, whereas maps, figures and tables produced by the analysis are written to their corresponding subdirectories under `data_output/`.

The directory structure itself can therefore be reproduced automatically after cloning the repository, while large source datasets and temporary files do not need to be distributed through GitHub.

# 3. Version control and GitHub

Version control is used to preserve the source code of the analysis and document the evolution of the project. The GitHub repository contains the reproducible Quarto workflow, project configuration and lightweight derived outputs, while large downloadable datasets, temporary files and private authentication credentials remain local.

This distinction is important because the objective is not to distribute copies of datasets that can be retrieved from their original providers, but to distribute the **code required to reconstruct the analysis**.

## 3.1. Files excluded from version control

Some files generated or used by the workflow should not be stored in the GitHub repository.

In particular, CORINE Land Cover rasters are relatively large and can be downloaded again from the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service. GISCO boundaries can similarly be reconstructed automatically. Temporary cache files are also unnecessary because they are generated during computation.

Finally, the Copernicus service key used for API authentication contains private credentials and must never be committed to the repository.

The following chunk creates the `.gitignore` file defining these exclusions.

```{r}
#| label: configure-gitignore

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Path to .gitignore
# ------------------------------------------------------------

gitignore_file <- here::here(
  ".gitignore"
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Define files excluded from Git
# ------------------------------------------------------------

gitignore_lines <- c(

  "# ========================================================",
  "# R / RStudio",
  "# ========================================================",

  ".Rhistory",
  ".RData",
  ".Ruserdata",
  ".Rproj.user/",

  "",

  "# ========================================================",
  "# Quarto temporary files",
  "# ========================================================",

  ".quarto/",
  "*_files/",
  "*_data/",

  "",

  "# ========================================================",
  "# Computational cache",
  "# ========================================================",

  "cache/",

  "",

  "# ========================================================",
  "# Copernicus CLMS authentication",
  "# NEVER COMMIT PRIVATE CREDENTIALS",
  "# ========================================================",

  "clms_service_key.json",

  "",

  "# ========================================================",
  "# Raw CORINE datasets",
  "# Keep directory structure but ignore downloaded data",
  "# ========================================================",

  "data_input/corine/**",
  "!data_input/corine/.gitkeep",

  "",

  "# ========================================================",
  "# Downloaded boundary data",
  "# Reconstructed automatically with giscoR",
  "# ========================================================",

  "data_input/boundaries/**",
  "!data_input/boundaries/.gitkeep",

  "",

  "# ========================================================",
  "# Operating-system files",
  "# ========================================================",

  ".DS_Store",
  "Thumbs.db"
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Write .gitignore
# ------------------------------------------------------------

writeLines(
  gitignore_lines,
  gitignore_file
)

cat(
  ".gitignore successfully configured.\n"
)
```

The `.gitignore` configuration separates **reproducible source code** from **reconstructable or private files**.

The directory `data_input/corine/` remains part of the project structure through its `.gitkeep` placeholder, but the actual CORINE files downloaded later are excluded regardless of their subdirectory. This is particularly useful here because CORINE data can be downloaded separately for Spain, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania before the three Baltic datasets are combined into a single **Baltic States study area** during the spatial analysis.

Similarly, GISCO boundaries are not versioned because they can be retrieved again automatically. The `cache/` directory contains only temporary computational products.

Most importantly, `clms_service_key.json` is excluded from Git. Each user must authenticate independently with the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service, so private credentials are never included in the reproducible repository.

## 3.2. Git and GitHub repository diagnostic

Creating a reproducible project structure is only useful if the source files are correctly tracked by Git and linked to the remote GitHub repository.

The following diagnostic therefore checks:

1.  whether the current project is a Git repository;
2.  which branch is currently active;
3.  whether a remote repository is configured;
4.  whether local files contain uncommitted modifications.

The chunk is deliberately read-only: it inspects the repository but does not commit, pull or push any files automatically.

```{r}
#| label: git-github-diagnostic

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Detect Git repository
# ------------------------------------------------------------

is_git_repository <- fs::dir_exists(
  here::here(".git")
)


if (!is_git_repository) {

  cat(
    "No Git repository was detected in the project root.\n"
  )

} else {

  cat(
    "Git repository detected.\n\n"
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Open repository
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  git_repository <- gert::git_open(
    project_root
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Identify current branch
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  git_branch <- gert::git_branch(
    repo = git_repository
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Identify configured remote repositories
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  git_remotes <- tryCatch(

    gert::git_remote_list(
      repo = git_repository
    ),

    error = function(e) {
      tibble::tibble()
    }
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Inspect working-tree status
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  git_changes <- gert::git_status(
    repo = git_repository
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Display diagnostic
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  cat(
    "Current branch:",
    git_branch,
    "\n\n"
  )


  if (nrow(git_remotes) > 0) {

    cat(
      "Configured remote repository:\n"
    )

    print(
      git_remotes
    )

  } else {

    cat(
      "No remote Git repository is currently configured.\n"
    )
  }


  cat(
    "\nWorking-tree status:\n"
  )


  if (nrow(git_changes) == 0) {

    cat(
      "No uncommitted changes detected.\n"
    )

  } else {

    print(
      git_changes
    )
  }
}
```

This diagnostic provides a simple reproducibility check without altering the repository. If a remote repository is listed, the local project is connected to GitHub. The working-tree status additionally indicates whether files have been modified since the most recent commit.

Uncommitted changes are not necessarily an error while the analysis is being developed; they simply indicate that the local version differs from the last version recorded by Git.

## 3.3. Protection of Copernicus credentials

The CORINE acquisition workflow requires authentication with the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service. Authentication is handled locally using a service-key file named `clms_service_key.json`.

Because this file contains private credentials, the workflow performs an additional security check before the API is accessed. Only the presence of the filename in `.gitignore` is verified; the credentials themselves are neither read nor displayed at this stage.

```{r}
#| label: verify-secret-git-protection

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Name of the local secret file
# ------------------------------------------------------------

secret_filename <- "clms_service_key.json"


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Read .gitignore
# ------------------------------------------------------------

gitignore_content <- readLines(
  here::here(".gitignore"),
  warn = FALSE
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Verify protection
# ------------------------------------------------------------

secret_is_ignored <- secret_filename %in%
  gitignore_content


if (secret_is_ignored) {

  cat(
    "Git protection check: OK\n",
    "The CLMS service-key file is excluded from version control.\n"
  )

} else {

  stop(
    paste0(
      "Security check failed: ",
      secret_filename,
      " is not listed in .gitignore."
    )
  )
}
```

If the diagnostic returns `Git protection check: OK`, the private Copernicus service-key filename is correctly excluded from version control.

Authentication itself is handled in the following data-acquisition section. This distinction is important for reproducibility: the workflow and authentication procedure are shared publicly, while **each user supplies their own private Copernicus credentials locally**.

## 3.4. Manual GitHub synchronization

Operations that modify the Git history are intentionally kept outside the automatic Quarto execution.

Rendering an analytical document should not automatically commit or push files to a remote repository. Doing so could unintentionally publish unfinished outputs or sensitive information. GitHub synchronization is therefore performed explicitly by the user after reviewing the changes.

A typical synchronization sequence is:

``` text
git status

git pull --rebase origin main

git add -A

git status

git commit -m "Update habitat fragmentation workflow"

git push origin main
```

The first `git status` identifies local modifications. `git pull --rebase` synchronizes the local branch with the remote repository before new changes are recorded. The files are then staged and reviewed again before creating the commit and pushing it to GitHub.

Consequently, the GitHub repository contains the **reproducible analytical workflow rather than the complete local working environment**. Large CORINE datasets, reconstructable GISCO boundaries, computational cache files and private Copernicus credentials remain outside version control.

This configuration completes the reproducibility setup. The next stage of the workflow retrieves the spatial datasets required for the analysis, beginning with authentication to the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service and automated acquisition of CORINE Land Cover data.

# 4. Data acquisition

This section prepares the spatial datasets required for the analysis.

The workflow relies primarily on **CORINE Land Cover (CLC)** data distributed by the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS). Five reference years are considered: **1990, 2000, 2006, 2012 and 2018**.

CORINE data are acquired separately for Spain, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania because the CLMS download service operates at country level. For the comparative analysis, however, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are subsequently treated together as a single **Baltic States study area**.

The data workflow follows four main stages:

1.  authentication to the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service;
2.  definition and verification of the required CORINE products;
3.  acquisition and local validation of the country-year rasters;
4.  retrieval of administrative boundaries and construction of the two study areas.

Downloaded raster data are stored locally under `data_input/corine/` and are excluded from Git because they can be reconstructed automatically from their original source.

## 4.1. CORINE Land Cover data source and Copernicus Land Monitoring Service authentication

CORINE Land Cover is used as the common land-cover dataset for the entire temporal analysis. The five selected status layers provide repeated observations spanning almost three decades while maintaining a common European classification system.

CORINE Land Cover data are retrieved programmatically from the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS). Access to the CLMS download API requires user authentication.

### 4.1.1. One-time user configuration

Authentication is the only preliminary step that cannot be reproduced directly from the GitHub repository because **each user must use their own Copernicus credentials**.

To reproduce the project on a new computer, the user must first:

1.  create or use an existing **EU Login** account;
2.  log in to the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service;
3.  generate a personal **CLMS service key** from the API-token interface;
4.  copy the complete JSON service-key information provided by CLMS;
5.  save it locally in the project root as:

`clms_service_key.json`

The resulting project structure should therefore contain:

``` text
habitat-fragmentation-europe/
│
├── workflow.qmd
├── clms_service_key.json      <- private local file
├── .gitignore
├── data_input/
└── data_output/
```

The service-key file contains private authentication information and must **never be uploaded to GitHub**. The project's `.gitignore` configuration explicitly excludes this file from version control.

A small one-time setup script can be used to create and validate the local credential file. This script only needs to be executed once per local installation. Once `clms_service_key.json` exists, the main Quarto workflow handles temporary authentication automatically.

The authentication procedure follows the CLMS API mechanism: the locally stored private key is used to sign a JSON Web Token (JWT), which is then exchanged for a temporary access token used by the download API.

The following optional code can be used to create the local credential file after the user has generated a CLMS service key and copied the complete JSON information provided by Copernicus.

This operation is required **only once per local installation**. It is deliberately not executed automatically when the Quarto document is rendered.

```{r}
#| label: one-time-clms-credential-setup
#| eval: false

# ============================================================
# ONE-TIME CLMS SERVICE KEY SETUP
# ============================================================
#
# Before running this chunk:
#
# 1. create or use an EU Login account;
# 2. log in to the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service;
# 3. generate a personal CLMS service key;
# 4. copy the complete JSON service-key information;
# 5. run this chunk manually once.


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Read service-key JSON from clipboard
# ------------------------------------------------------------

clipboard_text <- paste(
  readLines(
    "clipboard",
    warn = FALSE
  ),
  collapse = "\n"
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Validate JSON
# ------------------------------------------------------------

if (!jsonlite::validate(
  clipboard_text
)) {

  stop(
    paste0(
      "The clipboard does not contain valid JSON.\n",
      "Copy the complete CLMS service-key information ",
      "and run this chunk again."
    )
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Inspect required fields without displaying credentials
# ------------------------------------------------------------

service_key <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  clipboard_text
)

required_fields <- c(
  "client_id",
  "private_key",
  "token_uri",
  "user_id"
)

missing_fields <- setdiff(
  required_fields,
  names(service_key)
)

if (length(missing_fields) > 0) {

  stop(
    paste(
      "Invalid CLMS service key. Missing fields:",
      paste(
        missing_fields,
        collapse = ", "
      )
    )
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Verify RSA private-key structure
# ------------------------------------------------------------

if (!grepl(
  "BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY",
  service_key$private_key,
  fixed = TRUE
)) {

  stop(
    "The JSON does not contain a valid RSA private key."
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Save credential file locally
# ------------------------------------------------------------

secret_file <- here::here(
  "clms_service_key.json"
)

writeLines(
  clipboard_text,
  secret_file,
  useBytes = TRUE
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Remove sensitive values from the current R environment
# ------------------------------------------------------------

rm(
  clipboard_text,
  service_key
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Confirm creation without displaying credentials
# ------------------------------------------------------------

if (!fs::file_exists(
  secret_file
)) {

  stop(
    "The CLMS service-key file could not be created."
  )
}


cat(
  paste0(
    "Local CLMS service key created successfully.\n",
    "File: clms_service_key.json\n",
    "The credential content has not been displayed."
  )
)
```

Because this chunk is configured with `eval: false`, it is shown in the reproducible report but is not executed during rendering. Each user performs this setup manually using their own private Copernicus credentials.

The resulting `clms_service_key.json` file is then used by the authentication function defined in the following section.

### 4.1.2. Generate a temporary CLMS access token

The local service key configured in the previous step is used to generate temporary access tokens required by the CLMS data-request API. The following chunk verifies that the credential file is available and defines the authentication function used throughout the remainder of the data-acquisition workflow.

```{r}
#| label: clms-authentication
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Locate local CLMS service key
# ------------------------------------------------------------

clms_key_file <- here::here(
  "clms_service_key.json"
)

clms_credentials_available <- fs::file_exists(
  clms_key_file
)


if (!clms_credentials_available) {

  stop(
    paste0(
      "No CLMS service key was found.\n",
      "Create a personal CLMS service key and save it as:\n",
      "clms_service_key.json"
    )
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Function generating a temporary CLMS access token
# ------------------------------------------------------------

get_clms_access_token <- function(
  key_file = clms_key_file
) {

  # Read service-key JSON
  service_key <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
    key_file
  )


  # Verify required fields
  required_fields <- c(
    "client_id",
    "private_key",
    "token_uri",
    "user_id"
  )

  missing_fields <- setdiff(
    required_fields,
    names(service_key)
  )

  if (length(missing_fields) > 0) {

    stop(
      paste(
        "Invalid CLMS service key. Missing fields:",
        paste(missing_fields, collapse = ", ")
      )
    )
  }


  # Verify private key format
  if (!grepl(
    "BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY",
    service_key$private_key,
    fixed = TRUE
  )) {

    stop(
      "The CLMS private key is not recognised as an RSA PEM private key."
    )
  }


  # JWT validity period
  now <- floor(
    as.numeric(Sys.time())
  )


  claims <- jose::jwt_claim(
    iss = service_key$client_id,
    sub = service_key$user_id,
    aud = service_key$token_uri,
    iat = now,
    exp = now + 3600
  )


  # Write RSA key temporarily
  private_key_file <- tempfile(
    fileext = ".pem"
  )

  writeLines(
    service_key$private_key,
    private_key_file,
    useBytes = TRUE
  )


  rsa_key <- openssl::read_key(
    private_key_file
  )

  unlink(
    private_key_file
  )


  # Sign JWT
  jwt_grant <- jose::jwt_encode_sig(
    claim = claims,
    key = rsa_key,
    size = 256
  )


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# Exchange JWT for temporary access token
# ----------------------------------------------------------

response <- httr2::request(
  service_key$token_uri
) |>

  httr2::req_headers(
    Accept = "application/json"
  ) |>

  httr2::req_body_form(
    grant_type =
      "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer",
    assertion =
      jwt_grant
  ) |>

  # Wait up to one minute for CLMS
  httr2::req_timeout(
    seconds = 60
  ) |>

  # Retry transient connection/server failures
  httr2::req_retry(
    max_tries = 3
  ) |>

  httr2::req_perform()


  token_response <- httr2::resp_body_json(
    response,
    simplifyVector = TRUE
  )


  if (
    is.null(token_response$access_token) ||
    !nzchar(token_response$access_token)
  ) {

    stop(
      "CLMS authentication failed: no access token returned."
    )
  }


  token_response$access_token
}
```

The service key itself remains exclusively on the user's computer. The function only generates a temporary access token in memory, so neither the private RSA key nor the temporary authentication token is written into the Quarto document or GitHub repository.

### 4.1.3. Test the CLMS connection

Before interacting with the data-request API, the workflow tests whether a temporary access token can successfully be generated.

```{r}
#| label: test-clms-authentication

clms_access_token <- get_clms_access_token()

cat(
  paste0(
    "CLMS authentication successful.\n",
    "A temporary access token has been generated.\n",
    "The token is deliberately not displayed."
  )
)
```

If this message is returned, the local credentials are valid and authentication with CLMS is operational. The resulting access token can then be used by the data-request functions defined in the following sections. Because access tokens are temporary, the workflow can generate a new token from the local service key whenever necessary.

## 4.2. Required CORINE datasets

### 4.2.1. Dataset catalogue

The analysis uses the five CORINE Land Cover status layers corresponding to the selected observation years.

The CLMS identifiers are stored explicitly rather than being searched dynamically each time the document is rendered. This ensures that repeated executions refer to the same data products.

```{r}
#| label: clc-dataset-catalogue

clc_catalogue <- tibble::tribble(

  ~year,
  ~dataset_id,
  ~download_info_id,
  ~expected_name,

  1990,
  "8b393c8e474642d5acb4ed70fc2dc024",
  "fecff4c7-a5e5-428d-817d-a8ee5f23d99d",
  "CLC1990",

  2000,
  "6704f90ca82e4f228a46111519f8978e",
  "19d7fbd8-53ee-4d09-89b6-fe5231247763",
  "CLC2000",

  2006,
  "d443c86fec2f49e08ff12c7decdbf2af",
  "4841f8cb-6e7c-4227-bb35-cd787609c546",
  "CLC2006",

  2012,
  "a5ee71470be04d66bcff498f94ceb5dc",
  "b1027c88-6256-435b-98a3-62f019cbb381",
  "CLC2012",

  2018,
  "0407d497d3c44bcd93ce8fd5bf78596a",
  "7bcdf9d1-6ba0-4d4e-afa8-01451c7316cb",
  "CLC2018"
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Verify agreement with YAML years
# ------------------------------------------------------------

missing_catalogue_years <- setdiff(
  years,
  clc_catalogue$year
)

if (length(missing_catalogue_years) > 0) {

  stop(
    paste(
      "No CORINE dataset is configured for:",
      paste(
        missing_catalogue_years,
        collapse = ", "
      )
    )
  )
}


clc_catalogue
```

The catalogue separates the **analytical time parameters** defined in the YAML from the technical CLMS identifiers required to retrieve the corresponding products.

### 4.2.2. Country-year acquisition plan

The analysis contains two study areas but four source countries.

Spain is represented by one national dataset, while the Baltic study area is reconstructed from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

The `country_lookup` table defined during project initialization provides the correspondence between analytical ISO3 codes and the two-letter codes used in the local CLMS data structure.

```{r}
#| label: clc-acquisition-plan

clc_acquisition_plan <- tidyr::crossing(

  iso3 = country_lookup$iso3,

  year = years

) |>

  dplyr::left_join(
    country_lookup,
    by = "iso3"
  ) |>

  dplyr::left_join(
    clc_catalogue,
    by = "year"
  ) |>

  dplyr::arrange(
    study_area,
    iso3,
    year
  )


expected_clc_datasets <- 
  nrow(country_lookup) *
  length(years)


if (
  nrow(clc_acquisition_plan) !=
  expected_clc_datasets
) {

  stop(
    "The CORINE acquisition plan is incomplete."
  )
}


clc_acquisition_plan |>
  dplyr::select(
    study_area,
    iso3,
    clms_code,
    year
  )
```

The resulting table contains **20 expected country-year combinations**:

-   5 observations for Spain;
-   5 observations for Estonia;
-   5 observations for Latvia;
-   5 observations for Lithuania.

The three Baltic countries are retained separately during data acquisition but later merged analytically into one Baltic study area.

### 4.2.3. Existing local CORINE data

Before any new API request is submitted, the workflow checks whether the corresponding GeoTIFF already exists locally.

This avoids unnecessary network requests and makes repeated executions of the project much faster.

```{r}
#| label: initial-clc-inventory

find_clc_tif <- function(
  clms_code,
  year
) {

  year_folder <- here::here(
    "data_input",
    "corine",
    clms_code,
    as.character(year)
  )


  if (!fs::dir_exists(year_folder)) {

    return(
      NA_character_
    )
  }


  tif_files <- fs::dir_ls(
    year_folder,
    regexp = "\\.(tif|tiff)$",
    recurse = TRUE,
    type = "file",
    fail = FALSE
  )


  if (length(tif_files) == 0) {

    NA_character_

  } else {

    as.character(
      tif_files[[1]]
    )
  }
}


clc_inventory <- clc_acquisition_plan |>

  dplyr::mutate(

    tif_file = purrr::map2_chr(
      clms_code,
      year,
      find_clc_tif
    ),

    available =
      !is.na(tif_file)
  )


clc_inventory |>
  dplyr::select(
    study_area,
    iso3,
    clms_code,
    year,
    available
  )
```

This inventory is reconstructed directly from the files stored on disk. It therefore remains valid even after restarting R or reopening the project.

## 4.3. Automated CORINE acquisition

The following functions are required only when one or more expected CORINE datasets are missing locally.

The CLMS data-request service is asynchronous: a request is submitted, a task identifier is returned, and the task must then be monitored until the server has finished preparing the requested archive.

### 4.3.1. CLMS request functions

Several small functions are grouped together here because they form a single technical workflow:

**submit request → monitor task → download result**

```{r}
#| label: clms-request-functions


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper for optional values
# ------------------------------------------------------------

`%||%` <- function(x, y) {

  if (
    is.null(x) ||
    length(x) == 0
  ) {

    y

  } else {

    x
  }
}


# ============================================================
# Submit a CLMS request
# ============================================================

request_clc_download <- function(
  dataset_id,
  download_info_id,
  clms_code,
  token,
  output_format = "Geotiff",
  output_crs = "EPSG:3035"
) {

  request_body <- list(

    Datasets = list(

      list(
        DatasetID =
          dataset_id,

        DatasetDownloadInformationID =
          download_info_id,

        NUTS =
          clms_code,

        OutputFormat =
          output_format,

        OutputGCS =
          output_crs
      )
    )
  )


  response <- httr2::request(
    "https://land.copernicus.eu/api/@datarequest_post"
  ) |>

    httr2::req_headers(
      Accept = "application/json",
      Authorization =
        paste(
          "Bearer",
          token
        )
    ) |>

    httr2::req_body_json(
      request_body
    ) |>

    httr2::req_perform()


  result <- httr2::resp_body_json(
    response,
    simplifyVector = TRUE
  )


  task_id <-
    result$TaskID %||%
    result$task_id %||%
    result$TaskId %||%
    result$TaskIds$TaskID


  if (
    is.null(task_id) ||
    length(task_id) == 0
  ) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "No TaskID was returned for ",
        clms_code,
        "."
      )
    )
  }


  as.character(
    task_id[[1]]
  )
}


# ============================================================
# Check CLMS task status
# ============================================================

check_clms_task <- function(
  task_id,
  token
) {

  response <- httr2::request(
    "https://land.copernicus.eu/api/@datarequest_status_get"
  ) |>

    httr2::req_url_query(
      TaskID =
        task_id
    ) |>

    httr2::req_headers(
      Accept = "application/json",
      Authorization =
        paste(
          "Bearer",
          token
        )
    ) |>

    httr2::req_perform()


  httr2::resp_body_json(
    response,
    simplifyVector = TRUE
  )
}


# ============================================================
# Wait for task completion
# ============================================================

wait_for_clms_task <- function(
  task_id,
  check_every = 30,
  max_wait_minutes = 120
) {

  start_time <- Sys.time()

  # Generate first token
  token <- get_clms_access_token()

  token_start <- Sys.time()


  repeat {

    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Refresh token before its one-hour validity is reached
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    token_age <- as.numeric(
      difftime(
        Sys.time(),
        token_start,
        units = "mins"
      )
    )


    if (token_age >= 45) {

      token <- get_clms_access_token()

      token_start <- Sys.time()
    }


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Check task status
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    task_status <- check_clms_task(
      task_id =
        task_id,

      token =
        token
    )


    current_status <-
      task_status$Status %||%
      "unknown"


    cat(
      format(
        Sys.time(),
        "%H:%M:%S"
      ),
      "- Task",
      task_id,
      ":",
      current_status,
      "\n"
    )


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Successful completion
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    if (
      identical(
        current_status,
        "Finished_ok"
      )
    ) {

      return(
        task_status
      )
    }


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Failure
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    if (
      current_status %in%
      c(
        "Failed",
        "Finished_error",
        "Error",
        "Cancelled"
      )
    ) {

      stop(
        paste0(
          "CLMS task ",
          task_id,
          " failed. Status: ",
          current_status,
          "."
        )
      )
    }


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Timeout protection
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    elapsed_minutes <- as.numeric(
      difftime(
        Sys.time(),
        start_time,
        units = "mins"
      )
    )


    if (
      elapsed_minutes >
      max_wait_minutes
    ) {

      stop(
        paste0(
          "Maximum waiting time exceeded for CLMS task ",
          task_id,
          "."
        )
      )
    }


    Sys.sleep(
      check_every
    )
  }
}

# ============================================================
# Download completed result
# ============================================================

download_clms_result <- function(
  task_status,
  destination,
  timeout_seconds = 1800,
  max_attempts = 3
) {

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Verify successful CLMS task
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  if (
    is.null(task_status$Status) ||
    task_status$Status != "Finished_ok"
  ) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "The CLMS task is not ready. Current status: ",
        task_status$Status %||% "unknown"
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Verify download URL
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  if (
    is.null(task_status$DownloadURL) ||
    !nzchar(task_status$DownloadURL)
  ) {

    stop(
      "The task is finished but no DownloadURL was returned."
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Create destination directory
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  fs::dir_create(
    fs::path_dir(destination)
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Temporarily increase download timeout
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  old_timeout <- getOption("timeout")

  on.exit(
    options(timeout = old_timeout),
    add = TRUE
  )

  options(
    timeout = timeout_seconds
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Download with retry mechanism
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  download_successful <- FALSE


  for (attempt in seq_len(max_attempts)) {

    cat(
      "Download attempt ",
      attempt,
      " of ",
      max_attempts,
      "...\n",
      sep = ""
    )


    # Remove a partial file from a previous failed attempt
    if (fs::file_exists(destination)) {

      fs::file_delete(
        destination
      )
    }


    result <- tryCatch(

      {

        utils::download.file(

          url =
            task_status$DownloadURL,

          destfile =
            destination,

          mode =
            "wb",

          method =
            "libcurl",

          quiet =
            TRUE
        )

        TRUE
      },

      error = function(e) {

        message(
          "Download attempt failed: ",
          conditionMessage(e)
        )

        FALSE
      }
    )


    if (isTRUE(result)) {

      download_successful <- TRUE
      break
    }


    Sys.sleep(5)
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Verify successful download
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  if (!download_successful) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "CLMS download failed after ",
        max_attempts,
        " attempts."
      )
    )
  }


  if (!fs::file_exists(destination)) {

    stop(
      "The download completed but the destination file was not found."
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Report downloaded file size
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  file_size_mb <- as.numeric(
    fs::file_size(destination)
  ) / 1024^2


  cat(
    "\nDownload completed successfully.\n",
    "File: ",
    destination,
    "\n",
    "Size: ",
    round(file_size_mb, 2),
    " MB\n",
    sep = ""
  )


  destination
}
```

These functions contain no study-area-specific logic. They can therefore be reused for any European country supported by the same CLMS data service.

### 4.3.2. Download one country-year dataset

The next function links the generic CLMS API functions to the structure of this project.

For each country-year combination it first checks whether a GeoTIFF already exists. Only missing data trigger a new CLMS request.

```{r}
#| label: function-download-clc-country-year

download_clc_country_year <- function(
  clms_code,
  year,
  overwrite = FALSE
) {

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Find dataset information
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  dataset_info <- clc_catalogue |>
    dplyr::filter(
      .data$year == !!year
    )


  if (nrow(dataset_info) != 1) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "No unique CORINE dataset found for ",
        year,
        "."
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Define local paths
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  year_folder <- here::here(
    "data_input",
    "corine",
    clms_code,
    as.character(year)
  )


  fs::dir_create(
    year_folder
  )


  zip_file <- here::here(
    "data_input",
    "corine",
    clms_code,
    paste0(
      "CLC",
      year,
      "_",
      clms_code,
      ".zip"
    )
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Skip existing GeoTIFF
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  existing_tif <- find_clc_tif(
    clms_code =
      clms_code,

    year =
      year
  )


  if (
    !is.na(existing_tif) &&
    !overwrite
  ) {

    cat(
      "CLC ",
      year,
      " / ",
      clms_code,
      " already available locally. Skipping.\n",
      sep = ""
    )


    return(
      tibble::tibble(
        clms_code =
          clms_code,

        year =
          year,

        status =
          "already_available",

        task_id =
          NA_character_,

        tif_file =
          existing_tif
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Generate fresh token for request submission
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  token <- get_clms_access_token()


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Submit request
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  task_id <- request_clc_download(

    dataset_id =
      dataset_info$dataset_id[[1]],

    download_info_id =
      dataset_info$download_info_id[[1]],

    clms_code =
      clms_code,

    token =
      token
  )


  cat(
    "CLMS task submitted:",
    task_id,
    "\n"
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Wait for completion
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  task_status <- wait_for_clms_task(
    task_id =
      task_id
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Download ZIP archive
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  download_clms_result(
    task_status =
      task_status,

    destination =
      zip_file
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Extract archive
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  utils::unzip(
    zipfile =
      zip_file,

    exdir =
      year_folder
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Detect resulting GeoTIFF
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  tif_file <- find_clc_tif(
    clms_code =
      clms_code,

    year =
      year
  )


  if (is.na(tif_file)) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "The archive for ",
        clms_code,
        " / ",
        year,
        " was downloaded but no GeoTIFF was detected."
      )
    )
  }


  tibble::tibble(

    clms_code =
      clms_code,

    year =
      year,

    status =
      "Finished_ok",

    task_id =
      task_id,

    tif_file =
      tif_file
  )
}
```

The function is **idempotent**: an already available dataset is detected and skipped. This allows the workflow to be resumed after an interrupted acquisition without downloading completed datasets again.

### 4.3.3. Optional complete CORINE acquisition

The following chunk applies the previous function to every country-year combination that may be required.

It is intentionally configured with `eval: false`. Rendering the report should not automatically initiate up to twenty external download tasks.

A new user reproducing the project can execute this chunk manually once after configuring their own CLMS credentials.

```{r}
#| label: download-complete-clc-archive
#| eval: false
#| cache: false

clc_download_results <- purrr::map2_dfr(

  clc_acquisition_plan$clms_code,
  clc_acquisition_plan$year,

  function(clms_code, year) {

    tryCatch(

      download_clc_country_year(

        clms_code =
          clms_code,

        year =
          year,

        overwrite =
          FALSE
      ),

      error = function(e) {

        tibble::tibble(

          clms_code =
            clms_code,

          year =
            year,

          status =
            "error",

          task_id =
            NA_character_,

          tif_file =
            NA_character_,

          error_message =
            conditionMessage(e)
        )
      }
    )
  }
)


clc_download_results
```

The acquisition code therefore remains completely available and reproducible without being executed unnecessarily each time the HTML document is generated.

## 4.4. CORINE archive validation

### 4.4.1. Completeness check

After acquisition, the inventory is reconstructed from disk to confirm that all expected observations are available.

```{r}
#| label: validate-clc-archive

clc_inventory <- clc_acquisition_plan |>

  dplyr::mutate(

    tif_file = purrr::map2_chr(
      clms_code,
      year,
      find_clc_tif
    ),

    available =
      !is.na(tif_file)
  )


n_expected <- nrow(
  clc_inventory
)

n_available <- sum(
  clc_inventory$available
)


cat(
  "Expected CORINE rasters:",
  n_expected,
  "\n"
)

cat(
  "Available CORINE rasters:",
  n_available,
  "\n\n"
)


if (
  n_available ==
  n_expected
) {

  cat(
    "CORINE archive complete: all required datasets are available.\n"
  )

} else {

  missing_clc <- clc_inventory |>
    dplyr::filter(
      !available
    )


  warning(
    paste0(
      n_expected - n_available,
      " CORINE dataset(s) are missing."
    )
  )


  print(
    missing_clc |>
      dplyr::select(
        study_area,
        iso3,
        clms_code,
        year
      )
  )
}
```

For the current project, a complete archive contains **20 GeoTIFF files**: five observations for Spain and fifteen observations contributing to the Baltic States study area.

### 4.4.2. Raster technical validation

Before analysing landscape change, the rasters are checked for several technical properties that must remain consistent across the temporal series.

The validation verifies the coordinate reference system, spatial resolution and raster dimensions of all locally available datasets.

```{r}
#| label: validate-clc-raster-properties

get_clc_properties <- function(
  tif_file,
  study_area,
  iso3,
  year
) {

  r <- terra::rast(
    tif_file
  )


  tibble::tibble(

    study_area =
      study_area,

    iso3 =
      iso3,

    year =
      year,

    crs =
      terra::crs(
        r,
        proj = TRUE
      ),

    resolution_x =
      terra::res(r)[1],

    resolution_y =
      terra::res(r)[2],

    nrow =
      terra::nrow(r),

    ncol =
      terra::ncol(r)
  )
}


clc_raster_properties <- purrr::pmap_dfr(

  clc_inventory |>
    dplyr::filter(
      available
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(
      tif_file,
      study_area,
      iso3,
      year
    ),

  get_clc_properties
)


clc_raster_properties
```

The CORINE rasters used in the project are expected to use **ETRS89 / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035)** with a nominal raster resolution of **100 m**. This common projection is particularly useful for subsequent distance, area and regular-grid calculations.

A 100 m raster cell represents a nominal ground area of:

\[ 100 \times 100 = 10,000 m\^2 = 1 ha \]

although the effective thematic detail of CORINE is also influenced by its mapping methodology and minimum mapping unit.

## 4.5. Administrative boundaries and study areas

The CORINE rasters provide the land-cover information, but administrative boundaries are required to construct the geographic extents used for visualization and comparative analysis.

GISCO country boundaries are downloaded directly with `giscoR`, allowing them to be reconstructed without distributing additional shapefiles through GitHub.

The current `giscoR` documentation supports direct retrieval of country polygons in **EPSG:3035**, which matches the CORINE projection.

### 4.5.1. Download GISCO country boundaries

```{r}
#| label: download-study-boundaries

study_boundaries <- giscoR::gisco_get_countries(

  year =
    2024,

  epsg =
    3035,

  resolution =
    10,

  spatialtype =
    "RG",

  country =
    country_lookup$iso3,

  cache =
    TRUE,

  cache_dir =
    paths$boundaries
)


study_boundaries
```

GISCO returns an `sf` polygon dataset directly in the same projected coordinate system as the CORINE rasters. Country polygons can therefore be used for cropping, masking and constructing common study-area boundaries without an additional reprojection step.

### 4.5.2. Construct the two analytical study areas

The four downloaded country polygons are converted into the two geographical units defined by the research design:

-   **Spain**
-   **Baltic States**, combining Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

```{r}
#| label: construct-study-areas

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Add analytical study-area labels
# ------------------------------------------------------------

study_boundaries <- study_boundaries |>

  dplyr::left_join(

    country_lookup |>
      dplyr::select(
        clms_code,
        study_area
      ),

    by = c(
      "CNTR_ID" = "clms_code"
    )
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Verify country-to-study-area correspondence
# ------------------------------------------------------------

print(
  study_boundaries |>
    sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
    dplyr::select(
      CNTR_ID,
      ISO3_CODE,
      NAME_ENGL,
      study_area
    )
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Dissolve countries into the two analytical study areas
# ------------------------------------------------------------

study_areas_sf <- study_boundaries |>

  dplyr::filter(
    !is.na(study_area)
  ) |>

  dplyr::group_by(
    study_area
  ) |>

  dplyr::summarise(
    geometry = sf::st_union(geometry),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Display result
# ------------------------------------------------------------

study_areas_sf
```

The resulting object contains only two geometries. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania remain separate source countries for CORINE acquisition but are now dissolved into a common **Baltic States** spatial unit for the subsequent comparative workflow.

This completes the data-preparation stage. The next section explores the CORINE classification at the European scale before focusing on temporal forest dynamics within Spain and the Baltic States.

# 5. European CORINE Land Cover overview

Before focusing on the two study areas, the European CORINE Land Cover context is explored at the beginning and end of the study period.

This continental overview serves two purposes. First, it introduces the hierarchical CORINE classification used throughout the project. Second, it provides a common geographical context before moving to the more detailed comparison between Spain and the Baltic States.

Only **1990 and 2018** are used for this European overview. The intermediate observations (2000, 2006 and 2012) remain essential for the subsequent temporal analysis within the study areas, but downloading them for the whole of Europe would add unnecessary processing and storage for a purely contextual visualization.

The original 100 m CORINE data are preserved for analysis. Reduced-resolution copies are created only for interactive continental visualization in order to keep the Leaflet maps and resulting HTML document computationally manageable.

## 5.1. Pan-European CORINE datasets

### 5.1.1. European overview years

The European overview compares the two endpoints of the temporal series: **1990 and 2018**.

Both CORINE status layers are available as pan-European raster products at 100 m resolution in ETRS89 / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035).

```{r}
#| label: european-overview-parameters

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Years used only for the European contextual overview
# ------------------------------------------------------------

europe_overview_years <- c(
  1990,
  2018
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Local directory for pan-European CORINE data
# ------------------------------------------------------------

europe_corine_dir <- here::here(
  "data_input",
  "corine",
  "europe"
)

fs::dir_create(
  europe_corine_dir
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Display overview configuration
# ------------------------------------------------------------

tibble::tibble(
  parameter = c(
    "Overview years",
    "Original CLC resolution",
    "Original CRS"
  ),
  value = c(
    paste(
      europe_overview_years,
      collapse = " and "
    ),
    "100 m",
    "EPSG:3035"
  )
)
```

The pan-European rasters are stored separately from the country-level datasets used later for the detailed analysis. This avoids confusing contextual European data with the four country-specific temporal archives.

### 5.1.2. Download full pre-packaged European datasets

The CLMS data-request API distinguishes between custom spatial downloads and complete pre-packaged datasets.

Country-level CORINE data used previously were requested by specifying an area of interest. In contrast, the complete pan-European products are already prepared by CLMS and must therefore be requested through their corresponding **pre-packaged file identifiers**.

For pre-packaged datasets, the request contains only the dataset identifier (`DatasetID`) and the identifier of the prepared file (`FileID`). No custom output format, projection or spatial restriction is supplied because these properties are already defined by the pre-packaged product.

The two European overview datasets used here are the official **100 m GeoTIFF** products for 1990 and 2018 in version **V2020_20u1**.

```{r}
#| label: european-clc-prepackages

europe_clc_catalogue <- tibble::tribble(

  ~year,
  ~dataset_id,
  ~file_id,
  ~package_name,

  1990,
  "8b393c8e474642d5acb4ed70fc2dc024",
  "95232d29-1273-4336-89b0-bddf75a059bf",
  "u2000_clc1990_v2020_20u1_raster100m",

  2018,
  "0407d497d3c44bcd93ce8fd5bf78596a",
  "3d9e2413-46ca-4f6e-abf8-b6eb429a4e48",
  "u2018_clc2018_v2020_20u1_raster100m"
)

europe_clc_catalogue
```

The catalogue explicitly records the prepared raster files selected for the European overview. Keeping these identifiers in the workflow ensures that repeated executions refer to the same official CLMS products.

The following function submits a request for one pre-packaged CORINE file.

```{r}
#| label: function-request-clc-prepackage

request_clc_prepackage <- function(
  dataset_id,
  file_id,
  token
) {

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Pre-packaged CLMS request
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  request_body <- list(

    Datasets = list(

      list(
        DatasetID = dataset_id,
        FileID = file_id
      )
    )
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Submit request
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  response <- httr2::request(
    "https://land.copernicus.eu/api/@datarequest_post"
  ) |>

    httr2::req_headers(
      Accept = "application/json",
      Authorization = paste(
        "Bearer",
        token
      )
    ) |>

    httr2::req_body_json(
      request_body
    ) |>

    httr2::req_perform()


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Parse response
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  result <- httr2::resp_body_json(
    response,
    simplifyVector = TRUE
  )


  task_id <-
    result$TaskID %||%
    result$task_id %||%
    result$TaskId %||%
    result$TaskIds$TaskID


  if (
    is.null(task_id) ||
    length(task_id) == 0
  ) {

    stop(
      "The CLMS pre-package request returned no TaskID."
    )
  }


  as.character(
    task_id[[1]]
  )
}
```

Because the file has already been prepared by CLMS, this type of request is generally simpler than a custom spatial extraction. The server still returns a task identifier, which is monitored using the same task-status functions defined previously.

The next function manages the complete acquisition of one European CORINE year. It first checks whether the GeoTIFF is already available locally, then submits the pre-packaged request only when necessary.

```{r}
#| label: function-download-clc-europe-prepackage

download_clc_europe_year <- function(
  year,
  overwrite = FALSE
) {

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # 1. Identify selected pre-package
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  package_info <- europe_clc_catalogue |>
    dplyr::filter(
      .data$year == !!year
    )


  if (nrow(package_info) != 1) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "No unique European CLC pre-package found for ",
        year,
        "."
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # 2. Define local paths
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  year_folder <- fs::path(
    europe_corine_dir,
    as.character(year)
  )

  fs::dir_create(
    year_folder
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # 3. Detect existing GeoTIFF
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  existing_tifs <- fs::dir_ls(
    year_folder,
    regexp = "\\.(tif|tiff)$",
    recurse = TRUE,
    type = "file",
    fail = FALSE
  )


  if (
    length(existing_tifs) > 0 &&
    !overwrite
  ) {

    cat(
      "European CLC ",
      year,
      " already available locally. Skipping download.\n",
      sep = ""
    )

    return(
      invisible(
        existing_tifs
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # 4. Define outer CLMS download archive
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  outer_zip <- fs::path(
    europe_corine_dir,
    paste0(
      "CLC",
      year,
      "_Europe.zip"
    )
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # 5. Download only if outer archive is not already present
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  if (
    !fs::file_exists(outer_zip) ||
    overwrite
  ) {

    token <- get_clms_access_token()


    task_id <- request_clc_prepackage(

      dataset_id =
        package_info$dataset_id[[1]],

      file_id =
        package_info$file_id[[1]],

      token =
        token
    )


    cat(
      "European CLC ",
      year,
      " pre-package task submitted: ",
      task_id,
      "\n",
      sep = ""
    )


    task_status <- wait_for_clms_task(

      task_id =
        task_id,

      check_every =
        30,

      max_wait_minutes =
        120
    )


    download_clms_result(

      task_status =
        task_status,

      destination =
        outer_zip
    )

  } else {

    cat(
      "Existing CLMS download archive detected for ",
      year,
      ". Reusing it.\n",
      sep = ""
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # 6. Extract outer CLMS archive
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  utils::unzip(
    zipfile =
      outer_zip,

    exdir =
      year_folder
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # 7. Detect nested ZIP archives
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  nested_zips <- fs::dir_ls(

    year_folder,

    regexp =
      "\\.zip$",

    recurse =
      TRUE,

    type =
      "file",

    fail =
      FALSE
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # 8. Extract every nested ZIP
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  if (length(nested_zips) > 0) {

    cat(
      length(nested_zips),
      " nested ZIP archive(s) detected for CLC ",
      year,
      ".\n",
      sep = ""
    )


    purrr::walk(

      nested_zips,

      function(zip_file) {

        extraction_folder <- fs::path(
          fs::path_dir(zip_file),
          fs::path_ext_remove(
            fs::path_file(zip_file)
          )
        )


        fs::dir_create(
          extraction_folder
        )


        utils::unzip(

          zipfile =
            zip_file,

          exdir =
            extraction_folder
        )
      }
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # 9. Search recursively for GeoTIFF
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  tif_files <- fs::dir_ls(

    year_folder,

    regexp =
      "\\.(tif|tiff)$",

    recurse =
      TRUE,

    type =
      "file",

    fail =
      FALSE
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # 10. Validate extracted raster
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  if (length(tif_files) == 0) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "European CLC ",
        year,
        " was downloaded and archives were extracted, ",
        "but no GeoTIFF was detected."
      )
    )
  }


  cat(
    "\nEuropean CLC ",
    year,
    " successfully prepared.\n",
    length(tif_files),
    " GeoTIFF file(s) detected.\n",
    sep = ""
  )


  print(
    tif_files
  )


  invisible(
    tif_files
  )
}
```

The function is designed to be safely rerun. If the European raster already exists locally, the download is skipped unless `overwrite = TRUE` is explicitly requested.

The two European products can now be downloaded with the following chunk.

```{r}
#| label: download-european-clc
#| eval: false
#| cache: false
#| results: hide

purrr::walk(
  europe_overview_years,
  download_clc_europe_year
)
```

This chunk is intentionally excluded from automatic rendering because the download only needs to be performed once. A user reproducing the project can execute it manually after configuring their own CLMS credentials.

Once both archives have been downloaded and extracted, the project should contain pan-European CORINE rasters under:

``` text
data_input/
└── corine/
    └── europe/
        ├── 1990/
        │   └── ... U2000_CLC1990_V2020_20u1.tif
        │
        └── 2018/
            └── ... U2018_CLC2018_V2020_20u1.tif
```

### 5.1.3. Load pan-European CORINE rasters

Depending on the CLMS archive structure, a complete European dataset may contain either one raster or several tiled GeoTIFF files.

The following function handles both situations. When several tiles are present, they are combined virtually without first writing a new massive raster to disk.

```{r}
#| label: function-load-clc-europe

load_clc_europe <- function(year) {

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Locate the extracted folder for the requested year
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  year_folder <- fs::path(
    europe_corine_dir,
    as.character(year)
  )


  if (!fs::dir_exists(year_folder)) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "No European CORINE folder found for ",
        year,
        "."
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Find all GeoTIFF files recursively
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  tif_files <- fs::dir_ls(
    year_folder,
    regexp = "\\.(tif|tiff)$",
    recurse = TRUE,
    type = "file",
    fail = FALSE
  )


  if (length(tif_files) == 0) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "No European CORINE GeoTIFF found for ",
        year,
        "."
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Exclude French overseas department rasters
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  continental_tifs <- tif_files[
    !stringr::str_detect(
      tif_files,
      "French_DOMs"
    )
  ]


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Select the main European raster
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  expected_pattern <- paste0(
    "U",
    ifelse(year == 1990, "2000", year),
    "_CLC",
    year,
    "_V2020_20u1\\.tif$"
  )


  main_tif <- continental_tifs[
    stringr::str_detect(
      basename(continental_tifs),
      expected_pattern
    )
  ]


  if (length(main_tif) != 1) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "Could not uniquely identify the main European CLC raster for ",
        year,
        "."
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Load raster
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  terra::rast(
    main_tif[[1]]
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: load-european-clc
#| cache: false
#| results: hide
#| message: false
#| warning: false

clc_europe_1990 <- load_clc_europe(
  1990
)

clc_europe_2018 <- load_clc_europe(
  2018
)
```

```{r}
#| label: validate-european-clc

europe_clc_validation <- tibble::tibble(

  year = c(
    1990,
    2018
  ),

  resolution_x = c(
    terra::res(clc_europe_1990)[1],
    terra::res(clc_europe_2018)[1]
  ),

  resolution_y = c(
    terra::res(clc_europe_1990)[2],
    terra::res(clc_europe_2018)[2]
  ),

  nrow = c(
    terra::nrow(clc_europe_1990),
    terra::nrow(clc_europe_2018)
  ),

  ncol = c(
    terra::ncol(clc_europe_1990),
    terra::ncol(clc_europe_2018)
  ),

  crs = c(
    terra::crs(
      clc_europe_1990,
      proj = TRUE
    ),
    terra::crs(
      clc_europe_2018,
      proj = TRUE
    )
  )
)

europe_clc_validation
```

The two pan-European CORINE rasters are loaded from the locally extracted pre-packaged products. For 2018, additional GeoTIFF files representing French overseas departments are included in the archive; these are excluded from the continental European overview. The main European rasters are retained at their original 100 m resolution and EPSG:3035 projection.

## 5.2. CORINE classification

CORINE Land Cover uses a hierarchical nomenclature.

At **Level 1**, the classification contains five broad categories:

1.  Artificial surfaces;
2.  Agricultural areas;
3.  Forest and semi-natural areas;
4.  Wetlands;
5.  Water bodies.

At **Level 3**, these broad categories are subdivided into **44 detailed land-cover classes**. The forest habitat analysed later in the project corresponds specifically to classes **311, 312 and 313**.

An important technical characteristic of the downloaded CLC rasters is that their cell values do not directly contain the official three-digit CLC codes. Instead, values `1–44` correspond sequentially to the 44 Level-3 classes. Consequently, an explicit lookup table is required before any reclassification or ecological analysis.

### 5.2.1. Level-3 nomenclature and raster encoding

The following table defines the correspondence between the internal raster encoding, official CLC codes, Level-1 categories, class names and visualization colours.
