### 6.4.4. Shiny server for forest dynamics

The following server logic updates the corresponding raster whenever the selected year changes.

As in the Level-3 interactive maps, the Leaflet basemap is created only once. `leafletProxy()` then replaces the raster layer without recreating the complete widget, which keeps interaction responsive.

```{r}
#| label: shiny-forest-server
#| context: server
#| cache: false
#| echo: false

# ============================================================
# SPAIN
# ============================================================

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Create Spanish forest map once
# ------------------------------------------------------------

output$spain_forest_map <- renderLeaflet({

  leaflet() |>
    addTiles()
})


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Update Spanish forest raster when year changes
# ------------------------------------------------------------

observe({

  req(
    input$spain_forest_year
  )


  selected_year <- as.character(
    input$spain_forest_year
  )


  selected_raster <- terra::unwrap(

    spain_forest_leaflet[[
      selected_year
    ]]
  )


  leafletProxy(
    "spain_forest_map"
  ) |>

    clearImages() |>

    clearControls() |>

    addRasterImage(

      selected_raster,

      colors =
        forest_map_palette,

      opacity =
        0.90,

      project =
        FALSE,

      maxBytes =
        20 * 1024 * 1024
    ) |>

    addLegend(

      position =
        "bottomright",

      colors =
        forest_map_colors,

      labels =
        forest_map_labels,

      title =
        paste0(
          "Forest landscape - Spain - ",
          selected_year
        ),

      opacity =
        1
    )
})


# ============================================================
# BALTIC STATES
# ============================================================

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Create Baltic forest map once
# ------------------------------------------------------------

output$baltic_forest_map <- renderLeaflet({

  leaflet() |>
    addTiles()
})


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Update Baltic forest raster when year changes
# ------------------------------------------------------------

observe({

  req(
    input$baltic_forest_year
  )


  selected_year <- as.character(
    input$baltic_forest_year
  )


  selected_raster <- terra::unwrap(

    baltic_forest_leaflet[[
      selected_year
    ]]
  )


  leafletProxy(
    "baltic_forest_map"
  ) |>

    clearImages() |>

    clearControls() |>

    addRasterImage(

      selected_raster,

      colors =
        forest_map_palette,

      opacity =
        0.90,

      project =
        FALSE,

      maxBytes =
        20 * 1024 * 1024
    ) |>

    addLegend(

      position =
        "bottomright",

      colors =
        forest_map_colors,

      labels =
        forest_map_labels,

      title =
        paste0(
          "Forest landscape - Baltic States - ",
          selected_year
        ),

      opacity =
        1
    )
})
```

The two maps therefore provide a simplified temporal view of forest structure complementary to the complete CORINE Level-3 visualization.

The Level-3 maps describe the broader land-cover context, whereas the forest maps isolate the ecological component analysed subsequently:

``` text
CORINE Level 3
        ↓
complete landscape composition

Forest–matrix representation
        ↓
forest habitat structure

Binary forest raster at 100 m
        ↓
landscape fragmentation metrics
```

This distinction ensures that the interactive visualization remains intuitive while the quantitative analysis continues to use the original-resolution binary forest products.

## 6.5. Standardized landscape-analysis grid

Landscape fragmentation metrics depend strongly on the spatial unit within which they are calculated. Direct comparison of administrative units would introduce substantial differences in area and geometry between mainland Spain and the Baltic States. The analysis therefore uses a **regular grid** providing a common spatial support across both study areas.

A cell size of **25 × 25 km** is used throughout the analysis. With the original CORINE resolution of 100 m, a complete landscape unit contains:

\[ 250 \times 250 = 62,500 \]

CORINE raster cells, corresponding to a theoretical area of:

\[ 25 \times 25 = 625 km\^2 \]

This scale provides enough spatial context to characterize forest amount, patch structure and connectivity while remaining sufficiently fine to preserve substantial within-region variation.

The grid is constructed in **ETRS89 / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035)**, which is also the native projected coordinate reference system of the CORINE datasets used in this project. Because EPSG:3035 is an equal-area European projection expressed in metres, it is particularly appropriate for constructing equal-sized landscape units and calculating terrestrial surface areas.

Grid cells are not clipped to administrative boundaries. Each retained analytical unit remains a complete **25 × 25 km square**, thereby preserving a constant geometrical support through time.

However, cells situated along coastlines or external study-area boundaries may contain substantial areas outside the terrestrial study area. Such cells would provide a much smaller effective landscape than inland cells. To limit this edge effect, only grid cells containing at least **50% terrestrial study-area surface** are retained as potential analytical units.

The same procedure and threshold are applied to mainland Spain and the Baltic States.

### 6.5.1. Define the landscape-unit parameters

The principal characteristics of the analytical grid are first derived from the `grid_km` parameter defined in the YAML header.

```{r}
#| label: define-landscape-grid-parameters
#| cache: false

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Landscape-unit dimensions
# ------------------------------------------------------------

grid_size_m <- grid_km * 1000

grid_cell_area_km2 <-
  (grid_size_m^2) / 1e6


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Minimum proportion of terrestrial study area
# ------------------------------------------------------------

minimum_land_fraction <- 0.50


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# CORINE spatial resolution
# ------------------------------------------------------------

corine_resolution_m <- 100


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Number of CORINE cells represented by one complete grid cell
# ------------------------------------------------------------

pixels_per_grid_side <-
  grid_size_m /
  corine_resolution_m

pixels_per_complete_grid <-
  pixels_per_grid_side^2


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration summary
# ------------------------------------------------------------

grid_parameters <- tibble::tibble(

  parameter = c(
    "Grid-cell width",
    "Grid-cell height",
    "Theoretical cell area",
    "CORINE resolution",
    "CORINE cells per grid side",
    "CORINE cells per complete landscape unit",
    "Minimum terrestrial fraction"
  ),

  value = c(
    paste0(
      grid_km,
      " km"
    ),

    paste0(
      grid_km,
      " km"
    ),

    paste0(
      grid_cell_area_km2,
      " km²"
    ),

    paste0(
      corine_resolution_m,
      " m"
    ),

    as.character(
      pixels_per_grid_side
    ),

    format(
      pixels_per_complete_grid,
      big.mark = ",",
      scientific = FALSE
    ),

    paste0(
      minimum_land_fraction * 100,
      "%"
    )
  )
)


grid_parameters
```

For the current configuration, a complete landscape unit measures **625 km²** and contains approximately **62,500 original CORINE pixels**.

The grid size is parameterized rather than hard-coded throughout the workflow. Consequently, another landscape-unit size could later be tested by changing the YAML parameter without rewriting the grid-construction functions.

### 6.5.2. Prepare terrestrial study-area boundaries

The grid-selection procedure requires a terrestrial polygon representing each analytical region.

The spatial objects constructed previously in Section 6.1 are reused directly:

-   `spain_mainland_sf` represents mainland Spain after removal of the detached Spanish islands;
-   `baltic_states_sf` represents the combined Estonia–Latvia–Lithuania study area.

Both objects are validated and explicitly transformed to EPSG:3035 before grid construction.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-grid-study-area-boundaries
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# ============================================================
# MAINLAND SPAIN
# ============================================================

spain_grid_boundary <- spain_mainland_sf |>

  sf::st_transform(
    3035
  ) |>

  sf::st_make_valid() |>

  dplyr::summarise(
    geometry =
      sf::st_union(
        geometry
      ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# ============================================================
# BALTIC STATES
# ============================================================

baltic_grid_boundary <- baltic_states_sf |>

  sf::st_transform(
    3035
  ) |>

  sf::st_make_valid() |>

  dplyr::summarise(
    geometry =
      sf::st_union(
        geometry
      ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Validate coordinate reference systems
# ------------------------------------------------------------

cat(
  "Spain grid CRS: EPSG ",
  sf::st_crs(
    spain_grid_boundary
  )$epsg,
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)


cat(
  "Baltic grid CRS: EPSG ",
  sf::st_crs(
    baltic_grid_boundary
  )$epsg,
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

Both boundaries should report **EPSG:3035**. Using the same projected coordinate system as CORINE avoids unnecessary reprojection during the subsequent extraction of raster landscapes.

### 6.5.3. Function for constructing a standardized landscape grid

A reusable function is defined to construct the analytical grid from any projected study-area polygon.

The procedure follows six principal stages:

1.  determine the bounding box of the study area;
2.  align the grid origin to multiples of the selected cell size;
3.  generate complete square cells;
4.  retain cells intersecting the terrestrial study area;
5.  calculate the terrestrial proportion contained in each cell;
6.  retain cells satisfying the minimum terrestrial-area threshold.

Aligning the grid origin to multiples of 25 km ensures that grid placement is explicit and reproducible rather than depending arbitrarily on the exact lower-left coordinate of a national boundary.

```{r}
#| label: function-create-landscape-grid
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

create_landscape_grid <- function(
  study_boundary,
  study_area_name,
  cell_size = grid_size_m,
  minimum_fraction = minimum_land_fraction
) {

  # ==========================================================
  # 1. Retrieve study-area bounding box
  # ==========================================================

  bbox <- sf::st_bbox(
    study_boundary
  )


  # ==========================================================
  # 2. Align grid limits to multiples of cell size
  # ==========================================================

  xmin_aligned <-
    floor(
      bbox[["xmin"]] /
        cell_size
    ) *
    cell_size


  ymin_aligned <-
    floor(
      bbox[["ymin"]] /
        cell_size
    ) *
    cell_size


  xmax_aligned <-
    ceiling(
      bbox[["xmax"]] /
        cell_size
    ) *
    cell_size


  ymax_aligned <-
    ceiling(
      bbox[["ymax"]] /
        cell_size
    ) *
    cell_size


  # ==========================================================
  # 3. Construct aligned rectangular extent
  # ==========================================================

  aligned_bbox <- sf::st_bbox(

    c(
      xmin = xmin_aligned,
      ymin = ymin_aligned,
      xmax = xmax_aligned,
      ymax = ymax_aligned
    ),

    crs =
      sf::st_crs(
        study_boundary
      )
  )


  aligned_bbox_geometry <-
    sf::st_as_sfc(
      aligned_bbox
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # 4. Generate complete square grid
  # ==========================================================

  grid_geometry <- sf::st_make_grid(

    aligned_bbox_geometry,

    cellsize =
      c(
        cell_size,
        cell_size
      ),

    square =
      TRUE,

    what =
      "polygons"
  )


  complete_grid <- sf::st_sf(

    grid_original_id =
      seq_along(
        grid_geometry
      ),

    geometry =
      grid_geometry
  )


  # ==========================================================
  # 5. Retain cells intersecting study area
  # ==========================================================

  intersects_study_area <- lengths(

    sf::st_intersects(
      complete_grid,
      study_boundary
    )

  ) > 0


  candidate_grid <- complete_grid[
    intersects_study_area,
  ]


  # ==========================================================
  # 6. Intersect candidate cells with terrestrial study area
  # ==========================================================

  terrestrial_intersection <-

    suppressWarnings(

      sf::st_intersection(
        candidate_grid,
        study_boundary
      )
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # 7. Calculate terrestrial area within each grid cell
  # ==========================================================

  terrestrial_area <- terrestrial_intersection |>

    dplyr::mutate(

      terrestrial_area_m2 =
        as.numeric(
          sf::st_area(
            geometry
          )
        )
    ) |>

    sf::st_drop_geometry() |>

    dplyr::group_by(
      grid_original_id
    ) |>

    dplyr::summarise(

      terrestrial_area_m2 =
        sum(
          terrestrial_area_m2,
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),

      .groups =
        "drop"
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # 8. Attach terrestrial-area information
  # ==========================================================

  candidate_grid <- candidate_grid |>

    dplyr::left_join(

      terrestrial_area,

      by =
        "grid_original_id"
    ) |>

    dplyr::mutate(

      cell_area_m2 =
        cell_size^2,

      terrestrial_area_m2 =
        dplyr::coalesce(
          terrestrial_area_m2,
          0
        ),

      land_fraction =
        terrestrial_area_m2 /
        cell_area_m2,

      land_percent =
        land_fraction *
        100
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # 9. Apply minimum terrestrial-area threshold
  # ==========================================================

  analytical_grid <- candidate_grid |>

    dplyr::filter(

      land_fraction >=
        minimum_fraction
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # 10. Determine study-area identifier
  # ==========================================================

  study_prefix <- dplyr::case_when(

    study_area_name ==
      "Spain" ~ "ESP",

    study_area_name ==
      "Baltic States" ~ "BAL",

    TRUE ~ "GRID"
  )


  # ==========================================================
  # 11. Assign permanent analytical grid identifiers
  # ==========================================================

  analytical_grid <- analytical_grid |>

    dplyr::arrange(
      grid_original_id
    ) |>

    dplyr::mutate(

      study_area =
        study_area_name,

      grid_id =
        paste0(

          study_prefix,

          "_",

          stringr::str_pad(
            dplyr::row_number(),
            width = 4,
            pad = "0"
          )
        )
    ) |>

    dplyr::select(

      grid_id,

      study_area,

      grid_original_id,

      terrestrial_area_m2,

      land_fraction,

      land_percent,

      geometry
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # 12. Return analytical grid
  # ==========================================================

  analytical_grid
}
```

The function returns only complete square cells meeting the specified terrestrial-area criterion. Each cell receives a permanent identifier that can subsequently be used to link spatial units with landscape metrics and temporal observations.

### 6.5.4. Generate the Spanish and Baltic analytical grids

The same function and parameter settings are now applied independently to the two study areas.

```{r}
#| label: create-study-area-grids
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# ============================================================
# MAINLAND SPAIN
# ============================================================

spain_grid <- create_landscape_grid(

  study_boundary =
    spain_grid_boundary,

  study_area_name =
    "Spain"
)


# ============================================================
# BALTIC STATES
# ============================================================

baltic_grid <- create_landscape_grid(

  study_boundary =
    baltic_grid_boundary,

  study_area_name =
    "Baltic States"
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Report number of retained analytical units
# ------------------------------------------------------------

cat(
  "Retained Spanish landscape units: ",
  nrow(
    spain_grid
  ),
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)


cat(
  "Retained Baltic landscape units: ",
  nrow(
    baltic_grid
  ),
  "\n",
  sep = ""

```

The number of cells differs between the two regions because the study areas have different total surface areas. This does not affect comparability because every retained analytical unit follows the same grid geometry and terrestrial-area selection criterion.

### 6.5.5. Validate the analytical grids

Before the grid is used for sampling and landscape metrics, several properties are verified.

The diagnostic confirms:

-   the number of candidate landscape units;
-   the minimum, mean and maximum terrestrial proportion;
-   the coordinate reference system;
-   compliance with the 50% terrestrial-area criterion.

```{r}
#| label: validate-landscape-grids
#| cache: false

grid_validation <- dplyr::bind_rows(

  spain_grid |>
    sf::st_drop_geometry(),

  baltic_grid |>
    sf::st_drop_geometry()

) |>

  dplyr::group_by(
    study_area
  ) |>

  dplyr::summarise(

    n_landscape_units =
      dplyr::n(),

    minimum_land_percent =
      min(
        land_percent,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    mean_land_percent =
      mean(
        land_percent,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    maximum_land_percent =
      max(
        land_percent,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups =
      "drop"
  )


grid_validation
```

A second diagnostic verifies the CRS and range of terrestrial fractions explicitly.

```{r}
#| label: verify-grid-geometry
#| cache: false

grid_geometry_validation <- tibble::tibble(

  study_area = c(
    "Spain",
    "Baltic States"
  ),

  crs_epsg = c(

    sf::st_crs(
      spain_grid
    )$epsg,

    sf::st_crs(
      baltic_grid
    )$epsg
  ),

  number_of_cells = c(

    nrow(
      spain_grid
    ),

    nrow(
      baltic_grid
    )
  ),

  minimum_land_fraction = c(

    min(
      spain_grid$land_fraction,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    min(
      baltic_grid$land_fraction,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  ),

  maximum_land_fraction = c(

    max(
      spain_grid$land_fraction,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    max(
      baltic_grid$land_fraction,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )
)


grid_geometry_validation
```

The expected result is:

``` text
CRS = EPSG:3035

minimum_land_fraction >= 0.50
```

for both study areas.

Minor differences in terrestrial fraction are expected for cells situated near coastlines and external borders.

### 6.5.6. Visualize the standardized landscape units

The resulting grids are mapped together with the study-area boundaries to verify their spatial distribution.

The grid polygons themselves remain complete squares. The study-area boundary is displayed on top of the grid to reveal which units are affected by coastlines or external borders.

```{r}
#| label: map-landscape-grids
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 7
#| cache: false

# ============================================================
# MAINLAND SPAIN
# ============================================================

spain_grid_map <-

  ggplot2::ggplot() +

  ggplot2::geom_sf(

    data =
      spain_grid,

    fill =

  )


# ============================================================
# BALTIC STATES

baltic_grid_map <-

  ggplot2::ggplot() +

```

The map is primarily a methodological diagnostic. The full grid is not intended to imply that every retained cell will necessarily be used in the final landscape sample. Instead, it defines the common pool of standardized spatial units from which comparable forest landscapes can subsequently be selected.

### 6.5.7. Methodological interpretation and scale limitations

The standardized grid provides a common spatial framework for the subsequent fragmentation analysis. Each complete grid cell represents a theoretical area of **625 km²**, irrespective of its location in mainland Spain or the Baltic States.

Most importantly, the same grid geometry is maintained across all five observation years. Temporal changes in landscape metrics can therefore be attributed to changes in the mapped forest landscape rather than to changes in the spatial units used for measurement.

The 50% terrestrial-area criterion reduces the influence of highly incomplete coastal and border cells while preserving potentially relevant landscapes situated close to coastlines or external boundaries. The precise terrestrial proportion of every retained unit remains stored in the `land_fraction` attribute and can therefore be considered during subsequent landscape selection.

The choice of **25 × 25 km** represents a compromise between spatial detail and landscape context. With CORINE at 100 m resolution, each complete grid cell contains approximately **62,500 raster cells**, providing enough observations to characterize forest pattern while avoiding extremely large landscape units that could mask local spatial differences.

Nevertheless, the results remain scale dependent. Landscape metrics can vary according to both the **size** and **position** of analytical units. This constitutes a manifestation of the **modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP)**. A different grid size or a shifted grid origin could produce somewhat different values for patch density, edge density, largest-patch dominance or connectivity.

CORINE itself also introduces scale-related limitations. Although the raster product has a nominal pixel size of 100 m, the underlying CLC mapping methodology includes a minimum mapping unit and therefore cannot represent all fine-scale forest edges, narrow corridors or small clearings. Fragmentation measured from CORINE should consequently be interpreted as **landscape structure observable at the CORINE mapping scale**, rather than as the complete fine-scale ecological fragmentation of forest stands.

The 25 km grid should therefore be understood as a standardized and reproducible analytical framework rather than as a uniquely correct ecological scale.

In the following section, this grid is used to identify a limited number of comparable landscape units in each study area for detailed temporal analysis.

## 6.6. Literature-guided and reproducible landscape sampling

Calculating complete temporal landscape metrics for every grid cell would be possible, but the objective of the present analysis is to examine a limited number of local landscape trajectories in detail.

Selecting five cells completely at random across each entire study area would risk sampling landscapes unrelated to the forest processes motivating the comparison. Conversely, manually selecting cells after visually inspecting their trajectories could introduce substantial confirmation bias.

A **literature-guided, data-screened and reproducibly randomized sampling strategy** is therefore used.

The procedure separates three decisions:

1.  the scientific literature identifies the broad geographical and ecological context of interest;
2.  CORINE forest change between 1990 and 2018 identifies grid cells where the corresponding landscape process is actually detectable;
3.  five cells are then randomly drawn from this candidate pool using a fixed random seed.

This distinction is important because the expected trajectories remain hypotheses rather than predetermined results.

For Spain, the sampling is focused on **Catalonia in north-eastern Spain**. Long-term land-use reconstructions describe Catalonia as a Mediterranean forest-transition landscape where rural abandonment has allowed forests to recolonize former cropland and pasture. The sampling criterion therefore emphasizes **forest gain** rather than assuming generalized forest loss.

For the Baltic States, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania remain treated as a single analytical region. Remote-sensing studies have identified the Baltic countries as a hotspot of intensive forest use and high forest disturbance, but forest harvesting, subsequent regeneration and post-agricultural forest expansion can occur simultaneously. The Baltic sampling criterion therefore emphasizes **forest turnover**, defined here as the combined proportion of forest gain and forest loss between the two endpoint observations.

The selection procedure is performed only once. The resulting grid identifiers are subsequently retained unchanged for all five CORINE dates.

### 6.6.1. Define sampling parameters

To reduce remaining coastal and boundary effects, the final sample is restricted to cells containing at least **90% terrestrial study-area surface**, even though the broader analytical grid constructed previously retained cells from 50%.

A minimum initial forest proportion is also imposed so that landscape metrics are calculated in cells containing a meaningful forest component.

The final random selection uses a fixed seed, making the five selected cells fully reproducible.

```{r}
#| label: define-landscape-sampling-parameters
#| cache: false

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Number of final landscape samples per study area
# ------------------------------------------------------------

n_sample_cells <- 5


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Require nearly complete terrestrial landscape units
# ------------------------------------------------------------

sampling_minimum_land_fraction <- 0.90


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Minimum forest proportion in 1990
#
# This avoids selecting landscapes containing only negligible
# forest habitat.
# ------------------------------------------------------------

minimum_initial_forest_fraction <- 0.10


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Dynamic hotspot threshold
#
# Candidate cells are drawn from the upper 30% of the
# relevant forest-change distribution.
# ------------------------------------------------------------

dynamic_hotspot_quantile <- 0.70


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Fixed seed for reproducible random sampling
# ------------------------------------------------------------

sampling_seed <- 20260818


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Summary
# ------------------------------------------------------------

sampling_parameters <- tibble::tibble(

  parameter = c(
    "Final cells per study area",
    "Minimum terrestrial fraction",
    "Minimum initial forest fraction",
    "Dynamic hotspot quantile",
    "Random seed"
  ),

  value = c(
    as.character(
      n_sample_cells
    ),

    paste0(
      sampling_minimum_land_fraction * 100,
      "%"
    ),

    paste0(
      minimum_initial_forest_fraction * 100,
      "%"
    ),

    paste0(
      dynamic_hotspot_quantile * 100,
      "th percentile"
    ),

    as.character(
      sampling_seed
    )
  )
)


sampling_parameters
```

The 70th-percentile threshold does not directly determine the final sample. It only defines a sufficiently large pool of landscapes displaying relatively strong dynamics, from which the five final cells are randomly selected.

### 6.6.2. Retrieve the Catalonia sampling region

The Spanish case study is spatially constrained to Catalonia, corresponding to the broader north-eastern Spanish forest-transition landscape documented in the literature.

Rather than defining this region using arbitrary coordinates, its official NUTS-2 geometry is retrieved from GISCO. Catalonia corresponds to NUTS code `ES51`.

```{r}
#| label: retrieve-catalonia-boundary
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Retrieve Spanish NUTS-2 regions
# ------------------------------------------------------------

spain_nuts2 <- giscoR::gisco_get_nuts(

  year = 2021,

  epsg = 3035,

  resolution = 10,

  nuts_level = 2,

  country = "ES",

  cache = TRUE,

  cache_dir = paths$boundaries
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Select Catalonia
# ------------------------------------------------------------

catalonia_sf <- spain_nuts2 |>

  dplyr::filter(
    NUTS_ID == "ES51"
  ) |>

  sf::st_make_valid()


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Validate result
# ------------------------------------------------------------

if (nrow(catalonia_sf) != 1) {

  stop(
    paste0(
      "Catalonia could not be uniquely identified ",
      "from the GISCO NUTS-2 dataset."
    )
  )
}


cat(
  "Catalonia boundary successfully retrieved.\n",
  "CRS: EPSG ",
  sf::st_crs(catalonia_sf)$epsg,
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

Using an official regional boundary ensures that the geographical restriction is explicit and reproducible.

### 6.6.3. Construct endpoint forest-change rasters

Forest dynamics are summarized between the beginning and end of the study period.

Four mutually informative conditions are distinguished:

``` text
1990 = matrix, 2018 = forest → forest gain
1990 = forest, 2018 = matrix → forest loss
1990 = forest, 2018 = forest → persistent forest
1990 = matrix, 2018 = matrix → persistent matrix
```

For sampling purposes, Spain is screened primarily according to **forest gain**, while the Baltic States are screened according to **turnover**, defined as forest gain plus forest loss.

These variables are used only to identify candidate landscapes. They do not replace the five-date landscape metrics calculated later.

```{r}
#| label: create-endpoint-forest-change-rasters
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# ============================================================
# Function creating endpoint forest-change products
# ============================================================

create_forest_change_products <- function(
  forest_1990,
  forest_2018
) {

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Forest gain
  # 0 in 1990 → 1 in 2018
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  forest_gain <- terra::ifel(

    forest_1990 == 0 &
      forest_2018 == 1,

    1,

    0
  )


  names(forest_gain) <-
    "forest_gain"


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Forest loss
  # 1 in 1990 → 0 in 2018
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  forest_loss <- terra::ifel(

    forest_1990 == 1 &
      forest_2018 == 0,

    1,

    0
  )


  names(forest_loss) <-
    "forest_loss"


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Forest turnover
  #
  # Any endpoint transition between forest and matrix.
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  forest_turnover <- terra::ifel(

    forest_1990 !=
      forest_2018,

    1,

    0
  )


  names(forest_turnover) <-
    "forest_turnover"


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Return products
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  list(

    gain =
      forest_gain,

    loss =
      forest_loss,

    turnover =
      forest_turnover
  )
}


# ============================================================
# SPAIN
# ============================================================

spain_change_products <-
  create_forest_change_products(

    forest_1990 =
      spain_forest_binary_series[["1990"]],

    forest_2018 =
      spain_forest_binary_series[["2018"]]
  )


# ============================================================
# BALTIC STATES
# ============================================================

baltic_change_products <-
  create_forest_change_products(

    forest_1990 =
      baltic_forest_binary_series[["1990"]],

    forest_2018 =
      baltic_forest_binary_series[["2018"]]
  )
```

A forest turnover value of one therefore indicates that the endpoint forest status differs between 1990 and 2018. It does not specify whether the change represents permanent deforestation, temporary harvesting, regeneration or another land-cover transition.

### 6.6.4. Function for summarizing forest dynamics by grid cell

The 100 m binary forest rasters are now summarized within each 25 × 25 km landscape unit.

For each candidate grid cell, the function calculates:

-   forest proportion in 1990;
-   forest proportion in 2018;
-   forest gain proportion;
-   forest loss proportion;
-   total endpoint turnover;
-   net forest-cover change.

Because the binary raster contains `NA` outside the terrestrial CORINE domain, calculations use only valid terrestrial raster cells.

```{r}
#| label: function-summarize-grid-forest-change
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

summarize_grid_forest_change <- function(
  grid,
  forest_1990,
  forest_2018,
  change_products
) {

  # ==========================================================
  # 1. Combine all endpoint variables into a single raster stack
  # ==========================================================

  forest_stack <- c(
    forest_1990,
    forest_2018,
    change_products$gain,
    change_products$loss,
    change_products$turnover
  )


  names(forest_stack) <- c(
    "forest_fraction_1990",
    "forest_fraction_2018",
    "forest_gain",
    "forest_loss",
    "forest_turnover"
  )


  # ==========================================================
  # 2. Extract mean values for every grid cell in ONE operation
  # ==========================================================
  #
  # exact = TRUE is deliberately avoided here.
  #
  # The analytical grid uses 25 km cells and CORINE uses
  # 100 m cells. Because 25,000 m is exactly divisible by
  # 100 m, the grid geometry is already compatible with the
  # raster resolution and exact fractional-pixel calculations
  # are unnecessary for this screening step.
  # ==========================================================

  grid_statistics <- terra::extract(

    forest_stack,

    terra::vect(
      grid
    ),

    fun = mean,

    na.rm = TRUE
  )


  # ==========================================================
  # 3. Verify correspondence with input polygons
  # ==========================================================

  if (
    nrow(grid_statistics) !=
    nrow(grid)
  ) {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "Raster extraction returned ",
        nrow(grid_statistics),
        " rows for ",
        nrow(grid),
        " grid cells."
      )
    )
  }


  # ==========================================================
  # 4. Attach raster statistics to grid
  # ==========================================================

  grid |>

    dplyr::mutate(

      forest_fraction_1990 =
        grid_statistics$forest_fraction_1990,

      forest_fraction_2018 =
        grid_statistics$forest_fraction_2018,

      forest_gain =
        grid_statistics$forest_gain,

      forest_loss =
        grid_statistics$forest_loss,

      forest_turnover =
        grid_statistics$forest_turnover,

      net_forest_change =
        forest_fraction_2018 -
        forest_fraction_1990
    )
}
```

All change variables are expressed as proportions of valid terrestrial raster cells within each landscape unit.

### 6.6.5. Characterize forest dynamics across both grids

The previous function is applied to all admissible grid cells in both study areas.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-study-area-forest-change
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# ============================================================
# SPAIN
# ============================================================

cat(
  "Calculating forest-change statistics for Spain...\n"
)

spain_grid_dynamics <-
  summarize_grid_forest_change(

    grid =
      spain_grid,

    forest_1990 =
      spain_forest_binary_series[["1990"]],

    forest_2018 =
      spain_forest_binary_series[["2018"]],

    change_products =
      spain_change_products
  )


cat(
  "Spain completed: ",
  nrow(spain_grid_dynamics),
  " landscape units.\n\n",
  sep = ""
)


# ============================================================
# BALTIC STATES
# ============================================================

cat(
  "Calculating forest-change statistics for Baltic States...\n"
)

baltic_grid_dynamics <-
  summarize_grid_forest_change(

    grid =
      baltic_grid,

    forest_1990 =
      baltic_forest_binary_series[["1990"]],

    forest_2018 =
      baltic_forest_binary_series[["2018"]],

    change_products =
      baltic_change_products
  )


cat(
  "Baltic States completed: ",
  nrow(baltic_grid_dynamics),
  " landscape units.\n\n",
  sep = ""
)


# ============================================================
# SUMMARY DIAGNOSTIC
# ============================================================

forest_change_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(

  spain_grid_dynamics |>
    sf::st_drop_geometry(),

  baltic_grid_dynamics |>
    sf::st_drop_geometry()

) |>

  dplyr::group_by(
    study_area
  ) |>

  dplyr::summarise(

    mean_forest_1990 =
      mean(
        forest_fraction_1990,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    mean_forest_2018 =
      mean(
        forest_fraction_2018,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    mean_gain =
      mean(
        forest_gain,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    mean_loss =
      mean(
        forest_loss,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    mean_turnover =
      mean(
        forest_turnover,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    mean_net_change =
      mean(
        net_forest_change,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups =
      "drop"
  )


forest_change_summary
```

These summaries are diagnostic rather than inferential. Their purpose is to confirm that the endpoint change products contain meaningful spatial variation before the sampling criteria are applied.

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Save expensive intermediate grid statistics
# ------------------------------------------------------------

grid_dynamics_cache_dir <- fs::path(
  paths$cache,
  "grid_dynamics"
)

fs::dir_create(
  grid_dynamics_cache_dir
)


saveRDS(
  spain_grid_dynamics,
  fs::path(
    grid_dynamics_cache_dir,
    "spain_grid_dynamics.rds"
  )
)


saveRDS(
  baltic_grid_dynamics,
  fs::path(
    grid_dynamics_cache_dir,
    "baltic_grid_dynamics.rds"
  )
)


cat(
  "Grid-level forest dynamics saved to disk.\n"
)
```

### 6.6.6. Construct the Spanish candidate pool

The Spanish candidate pool is restricted to grid cells whose centroids fall within Catalonia.

Three additional conditions are then applied:

1.  at least 90% of the cell belongs to the terrestrial study area;
2.  forest occupied at least 10% of the valid landscape in 1990;
3.  forest gain belongs to the upper 30% of the eligible Catalonian distribution.

Using the cell centroid rather than merely spatial intersection prevents cells that only touch the Catalonian boundary from being classified as Catalonian landscapes.

```{r}
#| label: create-spain-sampling-pool
#| cache: false

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Determine whether grid-cell centroid lies in Catalonia
# ------------------------------------------------------------

spain_grid_centroids <-
  sf::st_centroid(
    spain_grid_dynamics
  )


inside_catalonia <- lengths(

  sf::st_intersects(
    spain_grid_centroids,
    catalonia_sf
  )

) > 0


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Initial eligible Catalonian cells
# ------------------------------------------------------------

spain_sampling_eligible <-
  spain_grid_dynamics[
    inside_catalonia,
  ] |>

  dplyr::filter(

    land_fraction >=
      sampling_minimum_land_fraction,

    forest_fraction_1990 >=
      minimum_initial_forest_fraction
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Calculate forest-gain hotspot threshold
# ------------------------------------------------------------

spain_gain_threshold <-
  stats::quantile(

    spain_sampling_eligible$forest_gain,

    probs =
      dynamic_hotspot_quantile,

    na.rm =
      TRUE
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Retain high-gain landscapes
# ------------------------------------------------------------

spain_sampling_pool <-
  spain_sampling_eligible |>

  dplyr::filter(

    forest_gain >=
      spain_gain_threshold
  )


cat(
  "Eligible Catalonian cells: ",
  nrow(spain_sampling_eligible),
  "\n",
  "High forest-gain candidate cells: ",
  nrow(spain_sampling_pool),
  "\n",
  "Forest-gain threshold: ",
  round(
    spain_gain_threshold * 100,
    2
  ),
  "%\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

This procedure does not force the selected cells to show net forest expansion. Instead, it increases the probability that the sampled landscapes contain detectable forest-regeneration dynamics relevant to the Spanish forest-transition hypothesis.

### 6.6.7. Construct the Baltic candidate pool

The Baltic case is treated differently because harvesting and regeneration can create both forest loss and gain within the same broader regional trajectory.

Candidate landscapes are therefore identified using **endpoint forest turnover** rather than net loss alone.

Cells must:

1.  contain at least 90% terrestrial study-area surface;
2.  contain at least 10% forest in 1990;
3.  belong to the upper 30% of the Baltic turnover distribution.

```{r}
#| label: create-baltic-sampling-pool
#| cache: false

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Initial eligible Baltic cells
# ------------------------------------------------------------

baltic_sampling_eligible <-
  baltic_grid_dynamics |>

  dplyr::filter(

    land_fraction >=
      sampling_minimum_land_fraction,

    forest_fraction_1990 >=
      minimum_initial_forest_fraction
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Calculate turnover hotspot threshold
# ------------------------------------------------------------

baltic_turnover_threshold <-
  stats::quantile(

    baltic_sampling_eligible$forest_turnover,

    probs =
      dynamic_hotspot_quantile,

    na.rm =
      TRUE
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Retain high-turnover landscapes
# ------------------------------------------------------------

baltic_sampling_pool <-
  baltic_sampling_eligible |>

  dplyr::filter(

    forest_turnover >=
      baltic_turnover_threshold
  )


cat(
  "Eligible Baltic cells: ",
  nrow(baltic_sampling_eligible),
  "\n",
  "High-turnover candidate cells: ",
  nrow(baltic_sampling_pool),
  "\n",
  "Turnover threshold: ",
  round(
    baltic_turnover_threshold * 100,
    2
  ),
  "%\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

The turnover criterion is deliberately neutral regarding change direction. A selected landscape can subsequently show forest expansion, forest contraction, patch coalescence, harvesting-related fragmentation, regeneration, or a combination of these processes.

### 6.6.8. Randomly select five landscapes from each candidate pool

The final selection is random within the two scientifically constrained candidate pools.

A fixed seed makes the result exactly reproducible.

```{r}
#| label: select-final-landscape-samples
#| cache: false

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Ensure that candidate pools are sufficiently large
# ------------------------------------------------------------

if (
  nrow(spain_sampling_pool) <
    n_sample_cells
) {

  stop(
    "The Spanish candidate pool contains fewer than five cells."
  )
}


if (
  nrow(baltic_sampling_pool) <
    n_sample_cells
) {

  stop(
    "The Baltic candidate pool contains fewer than five cells."
  )
}


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Set reproducible random seed
# ------------------------------------------------------------

set.seed(
  sampling_seed
)


# ============================================================
# SPAIN
# ============================================================

spain_sample <-
  spain_sampling_pool |>

  dplyr::slice_sample(
    n =
      n_sample_cells
  ) |>

  dplyr::arrange(
    grid_id
  ) |>

  dplyr::mutate(

    sample_id =
      paste0(
        "ESP_S",
        dplyr::row_number()
      )
  )


# ============================================================
# BALTIC STATES
# ============================================================

baltic_sample <-
  baltic_sampling_pool |>

  dplyr::slice_sample(
    n =
      n_sample_cells
  ) |>

  dplyr::arrange(
    grid_id
  ) |>

  dplyr::mutate(

    sample_id =
      paste0(
        "BAL_S",
        dplyr::row_number()
      )
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Combine final sample
# ------------------------------------------------------------

landscape_sample <-
  dplyr::bind_rows(

    spain_sample,

    baltic_sample
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Display selected landscape identifiers
# ------------------------------------------------------------

landscape_sample |>

  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>

  dplyr::select(

    sample_id,
    grid_id,
    study_area,
    land_percent,
    forest_fraction_1990,
    forest_fraction_2018,
    forest_gain,
    forest_loss,
    forest_turnover,
    net_forest_change
  )
```

The resulting ten grid identifiers constitute the fixed landscape sample used throughout the remainder of the project.

```{r}
    size =
      3
  ) +

  ggplot2::coord_sf(
    datum = NA
  ) +

  ggplot2::labs(

    title =
      "Baltic States",

    subtitle =
      "Random sample within high forest-turnover landscapes"
  ) +

  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +

  ggplot2::theme(

    panel.grid =
      ggplot2::element_blank(),

    axis.text =
      ggplot2::element_blank(),

    axis.title =
      ggplot2::element_blank(),

    axis.ticks =
      ggplot2::element_blank()
  )


# ============================================================
# COMBINED FIGURE
# ============================================================

spain_sample_map +

  baltic_sample_map +

  patchwork::plot_annotation(

    title =
      "Literature-guided and reproducible landscape sample"
  )
```

The candidate cells and final samples represent different stages of the selection process. Candidate cells satisfy the predefined geographical and forest-dynamic criteria, whereas the five outlined and labelled cells constitute the actual landscapes used for subsequent temporal landscape-metric calculations.

### 6.6.10. Sampling interpretation and limitations

The sampling strategy combines theoretical expectations with reproducible spatial selection while avoiding direct manual selection of individual landscapes.

For Spain, Catalonia provides a well-documented example of Mediterranean forest transition associated with rural abandonment and secondary forest expansion. Selecting among landscapes with relatively high observed forest gain therefore focuses the analysis on locations where this process can plausibly be examined without requiring every sampled cell to follow the same trajectory.

For the Baltic States, high forest turnover is used instead of forest loss because the regional forest system combines harvesting, regeneration and spontaneous forest expansion. A harvested forest stand may temporarily leave a CORINE forest class and later return to forest, while abandoned agricultural land may simultaneously undergo afforestation elsewhere.

Consequently, neither the Spanish nor the Baltic sampling criterion should be interpreted as proof of the causal processes proposed in the literature. The endpoint screening merely identifies landscapes where sufficient change occurred to make temporal landscape analysis informative.

A further limitation is that sampling is partly conditioned on observed 1990–2018 change. The resulting landscapes therefore represent **dynamic case-study landscapes**, not statistically representative samples of all forests in Spain or the Baltic States. Conclusions derived from the ten selected cells must consequently be interpreted as comparative case-study evidence rather than regional population estimates.

The fixed seed and explicit selection rules nevertheless ensure that the sample is fully reproducible and cannot be altered implicitly in response to the landscape-metric results.

## 6.7. Landscape metrics

The ten landscapes selected in Section 6.6 now constitute the spatial units used for the quantitative fragmentation analysis.

For each of the five CORINE observations (`1990`, `2000`, `2006`, `2012`, `2018`), the original **100 m binary forest raster** is extracted within each selected 25 × 25 km landscape unit. This produces a total of:

\[ 10 landscapes \times 5 dates = 50 landscape observations \]

Landscape metrics are calculated at the **forest-class level** rather than for the landscape as a whole. The objective is therefore to describe specifically the amount and spatial configuration of forest habitat relative to the surrounding terrestrial matrix.

The analysis uses eight complementary metrics:

| Metric       | Meaning                                                | Main interpretation for forest fragmentation     |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **PLAND**    | Percentage of landscape occupied by forest             | Forest habitat amount                            |
| **NP**       | Number of forest patches                               | Absolute patch subdivision                       |
| **PD**       | Number of patches standardized by landscape area       | Comparable fragmentation intensity               |
| **ED**       | Forest edge length per unit landscape area             | Edge complexity and fragmentation                |
| **LPI**      | Percentage occupied by the largest forest patch        | Dominance of the largest continuous forest block |
| **COHESION** | Structural connectedness of forest patches             | Physical aggregation and continuity              |
| **ENN_MN**   | Mean nearest-neighbour distance between forest patches | Spatial isolation                                |
| **AI**       | Proportion of maximum possible like adjacencies        | Degree of forest aggregation                     |

: Landscape metrics retained for the forest fragmentation analysis. {#tbl-landscape-metrics} These metrics are interpreted jointly rather than independently because different metrics can respond simultaneously to changes in forest amount and spatial configuration.

For example, forest expansion through patch coalescence could theoretically result in increasing `PLAND`, `LPI`, `COHESION` and `AI`, decreasing `ENN_MN`, and potentially decreasing `NP`, `PD` and `ED`. Conversely, fragmentation of an initially continuous forest may produce the opposite pattern.

These directions represent **interpretative hypotheses rather than expected results that the analysis is required to reproduce**.

### 6.7.1. Define patch connectivity and metric configuration

Raster patches must first be defined according to a neighbourhood rule.

An **8-neighbour rule** is used throughout the analysis. Forest cells sharing either an edge or a corner are therefore considered part of the same patch. This rule is kept constant for every landscape and every observation year.

The outer boundary of each 25 × 25 km analytical square is not counted as forest edge when calculating edge density. This prevents the arbitrary analytical border itself from artificially increasing forest edge length.

```{r}
#| label: define-landscape-metric-parameters
#| cache: false

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Patch connectivity
#
# 8 = queen's case:
# horizontal, vertical and diagonal neighbours are connected.
# ------------------------------------------------------------

patch_directions <- 8


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Forest class used internally for landscapemetrics
#
# The original binary rasters contain:
# 0 = matrix
# 1 = forest
#
# For landscapemetrics they will be recoded to:
# 1 = matrix
# 2 = forest
# ------------------------------------------------------------

landscape_matrix_class <- 1
landscape_forest_class <- 2


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Metrics retained for the analysis
# ------------------------------------------------------------

selected_metrics <- c(
  "pland",
  "np",
  "pd",
  "ed",
  "lpi",
  "cohesion",
  "enn_mn",
  "ai"
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Metric metadata
# ------------------------------------------------------------

metric_dictionary <- tibble::tribble(

  ~metric,     ~name,                           ~unit,                 ~fragmentation_interpretation,

  "pland",     "Percentage of landscape",       "%",                   "Forest habitat amount",
  "np",        "Number of patches",              "count",               "Absolute patch subdivision",
  "pd",        "Patch density",                  "patches / 100 ha",    "Area-standardized patch subdivision",
  "ed",        "Edge density",                   "m / ha",              "Density of forest-matrix edges",
  "lpi",       "Largest patch index",            "%",                   "Dominance of the largest forest patch",
  "cohesion",  "Patch cohesion index",           "%",                   "Structural connectedness",
  "enn_mn",    "Mean nearest-neighbour distance","m",                   "Isolation among forest patches",
  "ai",        "Aggregation index",              "%",                   "Aggregation of adjacent forest cells"
)


metric_dictionary
```

The metrics therefore cover three complementary dimensions of landscape structure:

``` text
COMPOSITION
    PLAND

PATCH SUBDIVISION AND EDGE
    NP
    PD
    ED
    LPI

AGGREGATION AND CONNECTIVITY
    COHESION
    ENN_MN
    AI
```

No single index is treated as a complete measure of fragmentation.

### 6.7.2. Prepare the selected 25 × 25 km raster landscapes

The original 100 m binary forest products generated in Section 6.3 are used here. The reduced-resolution rasters created for Leaflet visualization are never used for landscape metrics.

Each selected grid square is extracted independently for each observation year.

To avoid problems associated with persistent `SpatRaster` objects across R sessions, the 50 extracted landscapes are written to disk as GeoTIFF files under:

``` text
cache/
└── landscape_samples/
    ├── ESP_S1/
    ├── ...
    └── BAL_S5/
```

These intermediate rasters can therefore be reused in subsequent document executions without repeating the extraction.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-sampled-landscape-rasters
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: hide

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Cache directory for the 50 landscape observations
# ------------------------------------------------------------

sample_landscape_cache_dir <- fs::path(
  paths$cache,
  "landscape_samples"
)


fs::dir_create(
  sample_landscape_cache_dir
)


# ============================================================
# Function extracting one sample for one year
# ============================================================

prepare_sample_landscape <- function(
  sample_geometry,
  sample_id,
  study_area,
  year,
  overwrite = FALSE
) {

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Select the appropriate regional binary forest raster
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  source_raster <- if (
    study_area == "Spain"
  ) {

    spain_forest_binary_series[[
      as.character(year)
    ]]

  } else if (
    study_area == "Baltic States"
  ) {

    baltic_forest_binary_series[[
      as.character(year)
    ]]

  } else {

    stop(
      paste0(
        "Unknown study area: ",
        study_area
      )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Create sample-specific directory
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  sample_dir <- fs::path(
    sample_landscape_cache_dir,
    sample_id
  )


  fs::dir_create(
    sample_dir
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Output file
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  output_file <- fs::path(
    sample_dir,
    paste0(
      sample_id,
      "_",
      year,
      "_forest_landscape.tif"
    )
  )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Create file only when needed
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  if (
    !fs::file_exists(output_file) ||
    overwrite
  ) {

    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Crop the original 100 m forest raster to the complete
    # 25 × 25 km analytical square.
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    sample_raster <- terra::crop(

      source_raster,

      terra::vect(
        sample_geometry
      ),

      snap = "near"
    )


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Recode classes for landscapemetrics
    #
    # Original:
    # 0 = matrix
    # 1 = forest
    #
    # Analytical landscape:
    # 1 = matrix
    # 2 = forest
    #
    # NA remains NA.
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    sample_raster <- terra::ifel(

      sample_raster == 1,

      landscape_forest_class,

      terra::ifel(

        sample_raster == 0,

        landscape_matrix_class,

        NA
      )
    )


    names(sample_raster) <-
      "landscape_class"


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Write persistent GeoTIFF
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    terra::writeRaster(

      sample_raster,

      filename =
        output_file,

      overwrite =
        TRUE,

      datatype =
        "INT1U",

      NAflag =
        255,

      gdal =
        c(
          "COMPRESS=LZW"
        )
    )
  }


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Return filename rather than persistent SpatRaster pointer
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  output_file
}
```

The function returns the path to the derived GeoTIFF rather than keeping the raster itself as a persistent R object. This makes the workflow more robust between R sessions.

### 6.7.3. Create the complete 50-landscape raster inventory

The extraction function is now applied to every selected landscape and every year.

```{r}
#| label: build-sampled-landscape-inventory
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: hide

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Create all sample × year combinations
# ------------------------------------------------------------

sample_raster_inventory <- purrr::map_dfr(

  seq_len(
    nrow(
      landscape_sample
    )
  ),

  function(i) {

    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Retrieve one selected landscape
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    sample_row <-
      landscape_sample[
        i,
      ]


    sample_id_current <-
      sample_row$sample_id[[1]]


    grid_id_current <-
      sample_row$grid_id[[1]]


    study_area_current <-
      sample_row$study_area[[1]]


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Process all five years
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    purrr::map_dfr(

      years,

      function(year) {

        raster_file <- prepare_sample_landscape(

          sample_geometry =
            sample_row,

          sample_id =
            sample_id_current,

          study_area =
            study_area_current,

          year =
            year,

          overwrite =
            FALSE
        )


        tibble::tibble(

          sample_id =
            sample_id_current,

          grid_id =
            grid_id_current,

          study_area =
            study_area_current,

          year =
            as.integer(year),

          raster_file =
            raster_file
        )
      }
    )
  }
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Verify expected number of observations
# ------------------------------------------------------------

expected_landscape_observations <-
  nrow(
    landscape_sample
  ) *
  length(
    years
  )


if (
  nrow(sample_raster_inventory) !=
    expected_landscape_observations
) {

  stop(
    paste0(
      "Expected ",
      expected_landscape_observations,
      " sampled landscape rasters, but found ",
      nrow(sample_raster_inventory),
      "."
    )
  )
}


cat(
  "Sample landscape rasters prepared: ",
  nrow(sample_raster_inventory),
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)


sample_raster_inventory
```

The expected inventory contains exactly **50 rows**.

### 6.7.4. Validate raster geometry before calculating metrics

Landscape metrics based on distances, areas and edges require spatially consistent categorical rasters.

The following diagnostic checks resolution, coordinate reference system, raster dimensions and the number of valid terrestrial cells for every extracted landscape.

```{r}
#| label: validate-sampled-landscape-rasters
#| cache: false

sample_raster_validation <- purrr::map_dfr(

  seq_len(
    nrow(
      sample_raster_inventory
    )
  ),

  function(i) {

    inventory_row <-
      sample_raster_inventory[
        i,
      ]


    landscape_raster <- terra::rast(
      inventory_row$raster_file[[1]]
    )


    tibble::tibble(

      sample_id =
        inventory_row$sample_id[[1]],

      year =
        inventory_row$year[[1]],

      resolution_x =
        terra::res(
          landscape_raster
        )[1],

      resolution_y =
        terra::res(
          landscape_raster
        )[2],

      nrow =
        terra::nrow(
          landscape_raster
        ),

      ncol =
        terra::ncol(
          landscape_raster
        ),

      crs_epsg =
        terra::crs(
          landscape_raster,
          describe = TRUE
        )$code,

      valid_cells =
        as.numeric(
          terra::global(
            !is.na(
              landscape_raster
            ),
            "sum",
            na.rm = TRUE
          )[[1]]
        )
    )
  }
)


sample_raster_validation
```

A complete inland 25 × 25 km landscape should contain approximately **250 × 250 = 62,500 valid cells**. Slightly fewer valid cells are expected for the small number of selected landscapes intersecting a coastline.

All rasters should retain a resolution of **100 × 100 m** and EPSG:3035.

### 6.7.5. Calculate forest landscape metrics

A dedicated function calculates the selected metrics for one landscape observation.

Only the **forest class (`class = 2`)** is retained from the class-level metric outputs. Values describing the matrix are discarded because the ecological object of interest is forest habitat.

```{r}
#| label: function-calculate-forest-landscape-metrics
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

calculate_forest_landscape_metrics <- function(
  raster_file
) {

  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Load fresh raster from disk
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  landscape <- terra::rast(
    raster_file
  )


  # ==========================================================
  # COMPOSITION
  # ==========================================================

  metric_pland <-
    landscapemetrics::lsm_c_pland(

      landscape,

      directions =
        patch_directions
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # PATCH NUMBER AND DENSITY
  # ==========================================================

  metric_np <-
    landscapemetrics::lsm_c_np(

      landscape,

      directions =
        patch_directions
    )


  metric_pd <-
    landscapemetrics::lsm_c_pd(

      landscape,

      directions =
        patch_directions
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # EDGE STRUCTURE
  # ==========================================================

  metric_ed <-
    landscapemetrics::lsm_c_ed(

      landscape,

      count_boundary =
        FALSE,

      directions =
        patch_directions
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # DOMINANCE
  # ==========================================================

  metric_lpi <-
    landscapemetrics::lsm_c_lpi(

      landscape,

      directions =
        patch_directions
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # STRUCTURAL CONNECTIVITY
  # ==========================================================

  metric_cohesion <-
    landscapemetrics::lsm_c_cohesion(

      landscape,

      directions =
        patch_directions
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # PATCH ISOLATION
  # ==========================================================

  metric_enn <-
    landscapemetrics::lsm_c_enn_mn(

      landscape,

      directions =
        patch_directions
    )


  # ==========================================================
  # AGGREGATION
  # ==========================================================

  metric_ai <-
    landscapemetrics::lsm_c_ai(
      landscape
    )


  # ----------------------------------------------------------
  # Combine metric outputs
  # ----------------------------------------------------------

  dplyr::bind_rows(

    metric_pland,
    metric_np,
    metric_pd,
    metric_ed,
    metric_lpi,
    metric_cohesion,
    metric_enn,
    metric_ai

  ) |>

    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Retain forest class only
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    dplyr::filter(

      class ==
        landscape_forest_class
    ) |>

    dplyr::select(
      metric,
      value
    )
}
```

The use of `count_boundary = FALSE` for `ED` ensures that the artificial border of the 25 × 25 km analytical square is not interpreted as ecological forest edge.

### 6.7.6. Calculate metrics for all landscapes and years

The metric function is now applied to the complete raster inventory.

This produces:

\[ 10 landscapes \times
5 years \times
8 metrics = 400 metric observations \]

under ideal conditions.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-all-landscape-metrics
#| cache: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: hide

landscape_metrics_long <- purrr::map_dfr(

  seq_len(
    nrow(
      sample_raster_inventory
    )
  ),

  function(i) {

    inventory_row <-
      sample_raster_inventory[
        i,
      ]


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Calculate metrics
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    metric_values <-
      calculate_forest_landscape_metrics(

        raster_file =
          inventory_row$raster_file[[1]]
      )


    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # Attach landscape metadata
    # --------------------------------------------------------

    metric_values |>

      dplyr::mutate(

        sample_id =
          inventory_row$sample_id[[1]],

        grid_id =
          inventory_row$grid_id[[1]],

        study_area =
          inventory_row$study_area[[1]],

        year =
          inventory_row$year[[1]],

        .before =
          1
      )
  }
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Add descriptive metric metadata
# ------------------------------------------------------------

landscape_metrics_long <-
  landscape_metrics_long |>

  dplyr::left_join(

    metric_dictionary,

    by =
      "metric"
  )


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Display result
# ------------------------------------------------------------

landscape_metrics_long
```

This long-format table is the principal quantitative dataset used for the subsequent temporal analysis.
